a: Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the Israelites
p: Chapters 17–26 are often called the Holiness Code, for their refrain: be holy, for I am holy.
b: In 1877 the German scholar August Klostermann named Leviticus 17–26 the Heiligkeitsgesetz, the "Holiness Law," and the name stuck. These chapters speak to the whole people, not only to priests, and they keep saying "I am the LORD" and "be holy." Chapters 1–16 teach how the priests keep the sanctuary pure; chapters 17–26 teach how all Israel, and the land itself, must be holy. Scholars debate whether this was once a separate law book. Many critical scholars (Israel Knohl, Jacob Milgrom) think a "Holiness school" wrote it and also edited the older priestly material. Traditional readers see one book with two halves, both given at Sinai (25:1; 26:46; 27:34).

a: slaughters
p: In the camp, killing an ox, sheep or goat for meat had to happen at the altar.
b: The verb shachat means to slaughter by cutting the throat, the normal way of killing an animal for food or sacrifice. This law makes every killing of a domestic animal a sacrifice: meat may only be eaten as a peace offering, with the blood given at the altar (17:5–6). Deuteronomy 12:15, 20–21 allows Israelites who live far from the sanctuary to slaughter at home, as long as they pour out the blood. Rabbinic tradition explained the difference by time: in the wilderness all meat came from the altar, and Deuteronomy relaxed the rule for life in the land (Talmud, Chullin 16b–17a). Critical scholars debate which law came first, a key question for dating the priestly writings.

a: will have blood counted against him
p: Slaughter away from the altar is counted as shedding blood, the language used of murder.
b: "Blood will be counted to that man; he has shed blood." The same phrase "shed blood" is used of murder in Genesis 9:6. Jacob Milgrom argued that the law treats the killing of an animal for food as taking a life, which is allowed only when the blood goes back to God on the altar. Others read it more mildly: the man is guilty as if he had shed blood, because he cheated God of what belongs to him. Either way, an animal's life is not simply the owner's to take. Genesis 9:3–5 had already allowed meat but kept the blood back for God.
orig: דָּם יֵחָשֵׁב (dam yechashev), "blood will be counted"

a: he will be cut off from among his people
p: The penalty karet runs through these chapters. What it meant is debated.
b: The verb karat, "cut off," names a penalty that God himself carries out (20:3, 5–6 say "I will cut him off"). The rabbis listed thirty-six offenses that carry karet (Mishnah Keritot 1:1) and explained it as early death or dying without children, at God's hand rather than by a court. Some modern scholars add that the line of the guilty person ends, so that he is not "gathered to his people" after death (Milgrom). Others think it could mean being expelled from the community. The phrase "from among his people" fits all these readings. When a human court is meant, Leviticus says "must be put to death" (20:2, 9–16).
orig: וְנִכְרַת (venikhrat), "and he will be cut off"

a: out on the face of the field
p: Israelites, like their neighbors, sacrificed at local altars and in the countryside.
b: The law assumes people were killing animals as sacrifices "on the face of the field," at improvised altars or local shrines. Saul's army slaughtered on the ground and ate meat with the blood until Saul built an altar on the spot (1 Samuel 14:32–35). The books of Kings show many "high places," local hilltop shrines, until Hezekiah and Josiah closed them (2 Kings 18:4; 23:8). Leviticus 17 brings all sacrifice to one place, the tent of meeting, partly to stop sacrifice to other powers (17:7).

a: a soothing smell for the LORD
p: The phrase pictures God pleased and at rest, the same words used of Noah's sacrifice.
b: Reach nichoach sounds like the name Noah and means a smell that calms or soothes. It first appears when Noah sacrifices after the flood (Genesis 8:21) and runs through the offering laws. Ancient readers knew Mesopotamian flood stories in which the gods crowd around the sacrifice like flies; the Bible keeps the image of God smelling the offering but makes it a sign of his acceptance, not of hunger. Paul calls Christ's self-giving "as an offering and a sacrifice to God, a soothing smell" (Ephesians 5:2). In 26:31 God threatens not to smell Israel's soothing smells.

a: goat idols
p: The se'irim were hairy goat-shaped beings, perhaps demons of the wild places.
b: Se'irim means "hairy ones," the word for male goats. Here it names beings that people sacrificed to. Isaiah pictures se'irim dancing in ruined cities, next to desert creatures (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14), and Jeroboam set up priests "for the high places, for the goat idols and for the calves he had made" (2 Chronicles 11:15), where "goat idols" renders se'irim. So they were either idols in goat form or demons thought to live in the wild. The goat "for Azazel" sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement (16:8–10) belongs to the same world. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, renders mataiois, "empty things"; the KJV has "devils."

a: which they go after, prostituting themselves
p: Going after other gods is pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness.
b: The verb zanah, "act as a prostitute," is the Bible's strongest picture for worshiping other gods. It treats the covenant as a marriage and other worship as betrayal (Leviticus 20:5–6; Exodus 34:15–16; Judges 2:17). Hosea builds a whole book on the picture, and Ezekiel 16 and 23 tell Israel's history as a marriage gone wrong. The image is harsh to modern ears, but its point is that God's love is exclusive.

a: or any foreigner living among them
t: Laws for the foreigner, and Acts 15
p: Chapters 17–18 bind the resident foreigner too. Acts 15 seems to draw its rules for Gentiles from here.
b: Leviticus 17–18 repeatedly includes "the foreigner who lives among you" (17:8, 10, 12, 13, 15; 18:26). The rules that bind him are: no sacrifice away from the sanctuary, no eating blood, careful handling of animals that died or were torn, and the sexual laws of chapter 18. When the Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to keep away from "the pollution of idols, sexual immorality, what is strangled, and blood" (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25), many scholars see these same four laws, the ones Leviticus applies to foreigners living "in the midst" of Israel (Richard Bauckham). Others read the decree as a list of common pagan practices, or as part of the laws later rabbis gave all Noah's descendants.

a: I will set my face against that person
p: God himself, not a court, will act against the one who eats blood.
b: To "set the face" against someone is to turn toward him in hostility. In Leviticus God says it of eating blood (17:10), Molech worship (20:3, 5), turning to ghosts (20:6) and covenant breaking (26:17). The opposite is the priestly blessing, "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25). Ezekiel uses the same phrase often (Ezekiel 14:8; 15:7), one of many links between Ezekiel and the Holiness Code.
orig: וְנָתַתִּי פָנַי (venatatti panai), "and I will set my face"

a: For a body's life is in its blood
p: Nefesh here means the life that animates a body, not an immortal soul.
b: The KJV reads "the life of the flesh is in the blood" but then "atonement for your souls." Both words translate one Hebrew word, nefesh, which means a living being, its life or breath, or even the self. The verse is not about a soul separate from the body. It says that the life of a creature is carried in its blood, which is why blood belongs to God, the giver of life (Genesis 9:4–5; Deuteronomy 12:23). The same word appears three times in the verse: life of the flesh, your lives, and "by means of the life."
orig: נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם (nefesh habbasar baddam), "the life of the flesh is in the blood"

a: to make atonement for your lives
p: This is the Bible's clearest statement of why blood is used for atonement. Readers explain it differently.
b: Jacob Milgrom read the verse narrowly: it speaks of the peace offering just mentioned (17:5), and the blood "ransoms" the life of the man who killed the animal, so that the killing is not counted as murder. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, read it as a general principle behind all blood rites: God has given the life in the blood as a substitute for the worshiper's life (Gordon Wenham, Roy Gane). Hebrews builds on it: "no forgiveness comes about without blood being poured out" (Hebrews 9:22), and Christians see the principle fulfilled in Christ's blood (Romans 3:25; 1 John 1:7). After the Temple fell, the rabbis taught that prayer, repentance and acts of kindness atone in place of sacrifice (Hosea 14:2; Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4).

a: by means of the life in it
p: The little word be can mean "by means of" or "in exchange for."
b: The Hebrew banefesh joins the preposition be to "life." Read as "by means of," the blood atones because of the life it carries (KJV "for the soul" is a third possibility, "on behalf of the life"). Read as the be of price, as in "a life for a life," it says the blood atones as payment, a life in exchange for a life, which suits a substitution reading. Hebrew grammar allows both, and translations divide.

a: cover it with dirt
p: Jewish slaughter still covers the blood of birds and wild animals with earth.
b: Hunted animals could not be brought to the altar, so their blood is poured out on the ground and covered, giving it back to God as if to a grave. Jewish law still practices kisui hadam, covering the blood of a slaughtered bird or wild animal with earth or sawdust and saying a blessing. Kosher meat is also soaked and salted to draw out blood. Uncovered blood cries out: Abel's blood "has a voice" from the ground (Genesis 4:10), and Job pleads, "Earth, do not cover my blood" (Job 16:18; compare Ezekiel 24:7–8).

a: its blood is its life
t: The blood ban across the Bible
p: The ban on blood reaches from Noah to the church, and Jewish and Muslim food law still keep it.
b: God's first permission to eat meat keeps back the blood: "Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4). Since that law was given to Noah, many Jews and Christians have treated it as binding on all humanity, and Acts 15:20, 29 asks Gentile believers to keep it. Most churches later read the Acts rule as a temporary courtesy toward Jewish believers. Eastern Orthodox canons long kept it, and Jehovah's Witnesses apply it to blood transfusions. Islamic law also forbids blood (Qur'an 2:173). Jesus' words, "Anyone who is eating my flesh and drinking my blood has eternal life" (John 6:54), would have shocked hearers who knew this law, as John 6:60 shows.

a: an animal that died on its own or was torn by a wild beast
p: Hebrew nevelah and terefah: the source of the Yiddish word treif, "not kosher."
b: An animal that died on its own (nevelah) still has its blood in it, and one torn by a beast (terefah) has not been properly slaughtered. Exodus says, "Do not eat flesh torn by beasts in the field; throw it to the dogs" (Exodus 22:31), and Deuteronomy 14:21 lets an Israelite give a carcass to the foreigner or sell it to an outsider. Leviticus is milder: eating it makes a person unclean until evening, and he must wash. The Yiddish treif, for any non-kosher food, comes from terefah. Scholars note the different treatment of the foreigner in Deuteronomy and Leviticus as one sign of different law traditions.

a: he will carry his guilt
p: To "carry guilt" is to be answerable for it. Someone else can also carry it.
b: The phrase nasa 'avon means to bear the weight of a wrong and its consequences. Usually the guilty person bears it himself (5:1; 19:8; 20:17). But the same words describe the priests bearing Israel's guilt (Exodus 28:38; Leviticus 10:17), the goat carrying all Israel's guilt into the wilderness (16:22), and the servant of the LORD who "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). The phrase can also mean to forgive, to carry guilt away (Exodus 34:7).

a: I am the LORD your God.
t: The refrain of the Holiness Code
p: "I am the LORD" punctuates these chapters about fifty times, like a seal on each law.
b: Chapter 18 opens and closes with "I am the LORD your God" (18:2, 30), and the shorter "I am the LORD" ends many single laws (18:5, 6, 21). The formula recalls the opening of the Ten Commandments, "I am the LORD your God" (Exodus 20:2): the one who rescued Israel from Egypt has the right to set its laws. Ancient treaties also began by naming the great king. Chapter 19 uses the refrain after almost every law, as if each one were signed.

a: Do not do what is done in the land of Egypt
t: The customs of Egypt and Canaan
p: The list frames Israel against its neighbors. What did Egypt and Canaan actually practice?
b: Egyptian kings sometimes married their sisters or half-sisters, and the Greek Ptolemies who ruled Egypt after 305 BC made it a custom; Roman-era census papers show brother-sister marriage among ordinary Egyptians as well. Canaanite myth from Ugarit has the god Baal mating with a heifer, and Hittite law allowed sex with a horse or mule but punished it with a cow or sheep. The Sifra, the rabbis' midrash on Leviticus, says the "doings of Egypt" were these: "a man would marry a man, a woman would marry a woman, a man would marry a woman and her daughter." Many historians think the chapter paints the neighbors broadly, as polemic, rather than describing them fairly.

a: If a human being does them, he will live by them.
p: Ezekiel, Nehemiah, Jesus and Paul all quote this verse.
b: Ezekiel and Nehemiah recall these laws "which, if a person does them, he will live by them" to accuse Israel of rejecting them (Ezekiel 20:11, 13, 21; Nehemiah 9:29). Jesus tells a lawyer who has quoted the love commands, "Keep doing this, and you will live" (Luke 10:28). Paul quotes the verse twice to contrast the law's way with faith: "the person who has done these things will live by them" (Galatians 3:12; Romans 10:5). Readers of Paul divide. Some (Luther, Calvin) hear him saying no one can keep the law perfectly; many in the "new perspective on Paul" (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn) think he contrasts two eras or ways of belonging, not earning and grace.

a: he will live by them
t: Live by them, not die by them
p: From this phrase the rabbis drew the rule that saving a life overrides almost every commandment.
b: The Talmud reads "he will live by them" to mean "and not die by them" (Yoma 85b; Sanhedrin 74a). From this comes pikuach nefesh, the principle that saving a human life sets aside the Sabbath, the fasts and nearly every other law. A sick person must eat on Yom Kippur, and a doctor must break the Sabbath to save a patient. The rabbis named three exceptions a Jew must die rather than commit: idolatry, the forbidden sexual unions of this chapter, and murder. Earlier readers took "live" as long life in the land; later Jewish and Christian readers also heard eternal life (Targum Onkelos).

a: to expose nakedness
p: A Hebrew idiom for sexual intercourse, with a strong sense of shame.
b: "Uncover the nakedness of" (gillah 'ervah) is the Bible's main legal phrase for sex in these laws. 'Ervah means bare skin, the private parts, and also shame or exposure. The phrase recalls Ham, who "saw the nakedness of his father" (Genesis 9:22). Some scholars, reading Leviticus 18:7–8 (where a father's nakedness is the mother's), have argued that Ham's sin was with his mother (John Bergsma and Scott Hahn); most read Genesis 9 more simply. The Plain text keeps the idiom so readers can see how the law thinks of sex as belonging to a family's honor.

a: any close relative of his own flesh
p: The list covers relatives by blood and by marriage. It leaves out the daughter.
b: She'er besaro, "the flesh of his flesh," covers blood relatives, but the list also forbids in-laws: a father's wife, an uncle's wife, a daughter-in-law, a brother's wife. Marriage makes them "one flesh" with the family (Genesis 2:24). Oddly, the list never names a man's own daughter. Jewish interpreters said it was too obvious to state, or derived it from the ban on a woman and her daughter (18:17); some modern scholars think the list addresses a man about the women of his household as it was, and that a line has dropped out. The chapter speaks to men; women's own duties appear only in 18:23.

a: the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother
p: Does the law forbid two acts, or one? The little word "and" decides.
b: Read simply, the verse forbids sex with one's father and with one's mother. But the next words speak only of the mother, and 18:8 calls the father's wife "your father's nakedness." So many translations read the "and" as "that is": do not shame your father by lying with your mother (BSB). In the Talmud the majority reads "your father's nakedness" as the father's wife, while Rabbi Judah reads two separate offenses and counts sex with one's father as a crime of its own (Sanhedrin 54a). The Hebrew allows both; the Plain text keeps the "and."
orig: עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ וְעֶרְוַת אִמְּךָ ('ervat avikha ve'ervat immekha)

a: your father's wife
p: Sleeping with a father's wife was a bid for his place, and a famous scandal in the church.
b: Reuben "lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine" (Genesis 35:22), and Jacob's blessing takes away his firstborn rank: "you went up onto your father's bed" (Genesis 49:4). Absalom took David's concubines on the palace roof to claim his father's throne (2 Samuel 16:21–22), and Adonijah's request for Abishag cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13–25). Paul is appalled that a man in Corinth "has his father's wife," something not done even among pagans (1 Corinthians 5:1). Deuteronomy curses the man who does it (Deuteronomy 22:30; 27:20).

a: your father's daughter or your mother's daughter
p: Abraham married his half-sister. How could the patriarchs break these laws?
b: Abraham says of Sarah, "she is in fact my sister, my father's daughter though not my mother's" (Genesis 20:12). Jacob married two sisters (18:18), and Moses' father married his aunt (18:12). Tamar tells Amnon to ask King David for her, as if a half-sister marriage were still possible in his day (2 Samuel 13:13). The rabbis said the patriarchs kept the whole Torah before it was given (Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14), and Ramban answered that they kept it only in the land of Israel, which is why Jacob could marry sisters in Haran. Critical scholars see an older custom later forbidden. Christian readers often speak of a law given in stages.

a: your father's sister
p: Moses was born of a marriage that this law forbids.
b: Exodus says, "Amram took Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses" (Exodus 6:20; compare Numbers 26:59). The Septuagint of Exodus 6:20 makes Jochebed his cousin instead, perhaps to avoid the problem. The Bible does not hide that Israel's great lawgiver came from a union his own law would forbid, a sign that these laws were new or were not always kept.

a: your brother's wife
t: The brother's wife and the levirate
p: Deuteronomy commands what Leviticus forbids, in one case: a brother who died childless.
b: Leviticus forbids marrying a brother's wife (also 20:21), but Deuteronomy 25:5–10 commands a man to marry his brother's widow if the brother died without a son, to "raise up a name" for him, as in the stories of Tamar (Genesis 38) and Ruth. Jewish law reads Leviticus as the general rule and Deuteronomy as the one exception. John the Baptist condemned Herod Antipas for marrying Herodias, his living brother's wife: "The law does not allow you to have your brother's wife" (Mark 6:18). On Henry VIII, see 20:21.

a: It is a vile scheme.
p: Zimmah is planned, deliberate wickedness, especially sexual.
b: Zimmah comes from a verb meaning "to plan, plot." It names wrongdoing that is schemed, not slipped into, and in the law it is used for sexual wrongs: taking a woman and her mother (20:14), making a daughter a prostitute (19:29). The men of Gibeah's crime is called zimmah (Judges 20:6), and Ezekiel uses it again and again for Jerusalem's unfaithfulness (Ezekiel 16:27, 43; 23:21). The KJV has "wickedness," the BSB "depraved."

a: Do not take a woman as a rival to her sister
p: Jacob married sisters. The Dead Sea community read this verse as a ban on any second wife.
b: The plain sense forbids marrying two sisters while both live, which recalls Jacob, Leah and Rachel, whose rivalry fills Genesis 29–30. The word "rival" (litsror) echoes Hannah's rival wife in 1 Samuel 1:6. But the Hebrew "a woman to her sister" can also be an idiom for "one to another," as with the tabernacle curtains joined "to each other" (Exodus 26:3). The Damascus Document from Qumran accuses its opponents of "taking two wives in their lifetimes" (Damascus Document, column 4, lines 20–21), apparently reading this verse, with Genesis 1:27, as a ban on polygamy. Rabbinic law read it of sisters only, and allowed a man to marry his wife's sister after the wife's death.
orig: וְאִשָּׁה אֶל־אֲחֹתָהּ (ve'ishah el-achotah), "a woman to her sister"

a: while she is unclean with her monthly flow
p: Jewish family purity law still rests on this verse.
b: Chapter 15 says a man who lies with a woman during her period becomes unclean for seven days (15:24); here and in 20:18 the act is forbidden outright, with the penalty of being cut off. The rabbis reconciled the two by reading 15:24 as an accident. Ezekiel lists it among the marks of a righteous man that he does not approach a woman in her impurity (Ezekiel 18:6). Orthodox Jewish couples keep taharat hamishpachah, "family purity": no relations during the period and seven clean days after, then immersion in a mikveh, a ritual bath. Many Christians read the law as part of the purity code that no longer binds; some still follow it.

a: Do not give your seed in bed
p: The Hebrew stresses seed, the possibility of children. It links this law with the Molech law that follows.
b: Literally, "to your neighbor's wife do not give your lying for seed." The phrase shekhovtekha lezara appears again of animals (18:23; 20:15). Adultery is first of all a threat to the family line, since a child's father becomes uncertain. The next verse speaks of giving one's "seed" (zera, the same word, meaning children) to Molech. Many interpreters see a thread: chapter 18 guards the right use of seed, in sex and in children (Milgrom, Douglas). The adultery law itself is the Seventh Commandment, "You must not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14).

a: to make them pass over to Molech
p: A god or an offering? Children killed or dedicated? The rabbis and modern scholars divide.
b: Three questions divide readers. A god or an offering? Most scholars think Molech was a god, his name given the vowels of boshet, "shame" (John Day, George Heider). Otto Eissfeldt argued from Punic inscriptions that molk was a kind of sacrifice, so the phrase meant "as a molk offering." Killed or dedicated? The rabbis read "make pass" as a rite of dedication: the father handed the child to the idol's priests, who passed it between or over fires; he was liable only for both acts (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7; Talmud, Sanhedrin 64b; Maimonides, Avodah Zarah 6:3). Norman Snaith and Moshe Weinfeld argued for dedication too, noting that the Samaritan and Greek read "make serve" here (see the variant). Morton Smith and others answer with texts that speak plainly of slaughter and burning: Deuteronomy 12:31, Jeremiah 7:31, Ezekiel 16:20–21, Ezekiel 23:37–39 and Psalm 106:37–38. Foreign or Israelite? Jeremiah's protest that God never ordered it (Jeremiah 7:31) suggests some thought he had.
r: 20:2–5; Deuteronomy 12:31; Deuteronomy 18:10; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 32:35; Ezekiel 16:20–21; Ezekiel 23:37–39; Psalm 106:37–38

a: and do not treat the name of your God as common
p: Chillel means to make something holy ordinary. It is a key word of chapters 18–22.
b: The verb chillel, usually translated "profane," means to make common what is holy, to drag it out of God's sphere into the everyday. God's name, the Sabbath, the holy food, the priests and the sanctuary can all be "made common" (19:8, 12; 21:6, 9, 12; 22:2, 32). It is not the same as cursing God (24:11). The opposite is qiddesh, "make holy." Jewish tradition calls a public act that shames God chillul hashem and its opposite, honoring God even to death, kiddush hashem (from 22:32).

a: in the ways of lying down with a woman
p: The Hebrew is unusual: "you shall not lie with a male the lyings of a woman." What act is meant is debated.
b: Literally: "And with a male you shall not lie the lyings (mishkevei, plural) of a woman." The word "male" (zakhar) is the general word for a male of any age, not "boy" or "servant." The opposite phrase, "the lying of a male," appears in Numbers 31:17–18 and Judges 21:11–12 for a woman who has had sex with a man. From that parallel Saul Olyan argued that "the lyings of a woman" means the kind of intercourse a woman receives, so the verse forbids anal intercourse between men, and he thought it originally addressed the active partner only. Jewish law likewise defined the crime as that act (Talmud, Sanhedrin 54a–b). Others, including most traditional Christian readers, take the phrase more broadly: lying with a male as one would with a woman. The verse says nothing of women together.
orig: מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה (mishkevei ishah), "lyings of a woman"

a: It is abhorrent.
p: To'evah means something abhorred, a violation of the right order. Whether it is ritual or moral is debated.
b: To'evah (KJV "abomination") is something abhorrent to someone. It is used for unclean foods (Deuteronomy 14:3), for Egyptians' disgust at eating with Hebrews (Genesis 43:32), for idols and child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), for dishonest weights (Deuteronomy 25:16), and for pride, lying and murder (Proverbs 6:16–19). In this verse it is used of one act, but 18:26–30 calls all the acts of the chapter to'evot. John Boswell argued that the word marks ritual impurity tied to idolatry, not moral evil. Critics answer that the word often names plain moral wrongs, and that the whole chapter, including incest and adultery, is meant (Gagnon). Some scholars think the word marks what crosses boundaries, as in Mary Douglas's reading.

a: With a male do not lie down
t: How Jews and Christians have read 18:22
p: For most of history, synagogue and church read this verse as a lasting ban. That reading is still held by many.
b: Jewish tradition counts this among the arayot, the forbidden unions for which a Jew must die rather than sin. Philo and Josephus wrote that the law allows only the union of man and wife "according to nature" (Josephus, Against Apion 2.199). The rabbis applied "what is done in the land of Egypt" (18:3) to women's unions too, and Orthodox Judaism holds the ban today. Christian tradition, from the church fathers through Aquinas and the Reformers, read 18:22 as moral law, not ceremonial, because Paul seems to echo it: his word arsenokoitai (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10) is built from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, arsenos "male" and koitē "bed" (David Wright). Romans 1:26–27 adds women. The Catholic Catechism, Orthodox churches and most evangelical and global churches keep this reading.

a: It is abhorrent.
p: Since the 1950s some argue it forbids less than it seems; others answer that it forbids all male intercourse.
b: Derrick Sherwin Bailey (1955) and John Boswell (1980) tied the law to idolatry and cult prostitution (compare the qadesh of Deuteronomy 23:17–18 and 1 Kings 14:24). Saul Olyan (1994) limited it to anal intercourse; Jacob Milgrom agreed and held that it binds only Israelites and residents of the Holy Land. James Brownson (2013) argued that its logic is patriarchal shame and procreation, so it does not address faithful same-sex partnerships. Robert Gagnon answers that the ban is absolute, punishes both partners (20:13), rests on the male-female design of Genesis 1–2 (Matthew 19:4–6), and is repeated by Paul while the food laws are dropped. Revisionists reply that Acts 15:20, 29 also repeats the blood ban of 17:10–14 for Gentiles, which most churches set aside, and that Ezekiel 18:6 treats 18:19 as a moral mark too, so repetition alone does not settle what still binds. Each side accuses the other of reading its own world into the text.
r: 20:13; Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6; Romans 1:26–27; Acts 15:20, 29; Ezekiel 18:6; Deuteronomy 23:17–18; 1 Kings 14:24

a: It is a wrongful mixing.
p: Tevel, from a verb meaning "to mix," names the mixing of kinds that God made separate.
b: Tevel appears only here and in 20:12 (a man with his daughter-in-law). It comes from balal, "to mix," the word behind the confusion at Babel (Genesis 11:9). The KJV's "confusion" is close. The idea fits the chapter's and the book's concern with keeping kinds apart, as in the ban on mixed seed and mixed cloth (19:19). Bestiality is forbidden in every biblical law collection (Exodus 22:19; Deuteronomy 27:21), and this law alone addresses the woman directly. Hittite law punished sex with cattle, sheep, pigs or dogs by death but allowed it with a horse or mule; Herodotus reports a goat and a woman in Egypt (2.46).

a: The land became unclean
t: Past tense in a law for the future
p: God speaks of Canaan's expulsion as already done. Readers explain the tense differently.
b: The verbs here are past: the land "became unclean," God "called it to account," the land "vomited out" its people. Yet Israel is still at Sinai, and 18:24 says "I am driving out." Traditional readers take this as the prophetic past, a future so certain it can be told as done. Many critical scholars see a writer looking back after the conquest, or after Judah itself had been "vomited out" in exile, as 26:33–39 warns. Either way the logic is moral: the Canaanites did not lose the land by chance, and Israel can lose it the same way (18:28).

a: the land vomited out the people living in it
p: The land is pictured as a living body that cannot hold down wrongdoing.
b: Leviticus treats the land almost as a person: it becomes unclean, it rests and keeps Sabbaths (25:2; 26:34), and it vomits out those who defile it (18:28; 20:22). The picture goes back to the ground that swallowed Abel's blood and then refused Cain its strength (Genesis 4:10–12). Numbers 35:33–34 warns that bloodshed pollutes the land. Genesis 15:16 says Abraham's family would wait until "the guilt of the Amorites" was full. For many readers this explains the conquest as judgment, not mere seizure; for others it raises the hard question of why whole peoples were driven out.

a: keep what I have placed in your charge
p: The rabbis read this verse as a call to build safeguards around the commandments.
b: Mishmarti means "my charge," what I have given you to guard. The Talmud reads "you shall guard my guarding" as "make a guard for my guard" (Yevamot 21a): rabbinic rules that keep people far from the forbidden acts, such as extending the list of forbidden relatives to "secondary" relations. This is the idea behind "make a fence around the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 1:1). Christians sometimes accuse such fences of adding to God's law (Mark 7:8); Jewish teachers answer that a fence protects what is precious.

a: the whole community
t: Kedoshim: the heart of the Torah
p: The rabbis said most of the Torah's essentials hang on this chapter, and that it holds the Ten Commandments.
b: This is the only law in Leviticus addressed to "the whole community." The Sifra explains: it was spoken to everyone together because most of the Torah's main teachings depend on it. Leviticus Rabbah 24:5 shows that each of the Ten Commandments has an echo here: "I am the LORD your God" (19:3), no idols (19:4), no false oaths (19:12), the Sabbath (19:3), parents (19:3), and so on. The weekly reading that begins here is called Kedoshim, "holy ones." In Reform Judaism chapter 19 is read on the afternoon of Yom Kippur in place of chapter 18.

a: You will be holy, because I am holy
p: The verse makes holiness the people's calling, not only the priests'. 1 Peter quotes it.
b: Qedoshim tihyu: "holy you will be," plural, addressed to everyone. In Exodus Israel was called to be "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6); here that holiness is spelled out in daily life: respect for parents, care for the poor, honesty in business. Rashi took "be holy" as "keep yourselves apart" from the forbidden unions of chapter 18; Ramban read it more widely: do not be "a scoundrel within the bounds of the Torah," indulging in what is technically allowed. Jesus' "be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48) and "Become compassionate, the way your Father is compassionate" (Luke 6:36) follow the same pattern, and 1 Peter 1:15–16 quotes the verse directly.

a: Each of you is to fear his mother and his father
p: Fear here means reverence. And the mother comes first, unlike in Exodus.
b: The Ten Commandments say "honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12); here it is "fear," the same verb used for fearing God (19:14, 32). The rabbis spelled it out: fear means not sitting in a parent's seat or contradicting them; honor means feeding, clothing and caring for them (Talmud, Kiddushin 31b). They also noticed the order. Children tend to honor the mother more and fear the father more, they said, so the Torah puts the father first in honor and the mother first in fear, to teach that both deserve both (Kiddushin 30b–31a).

a: the no-gods
p: A pun: el is "god," elil is "nothing, worthless."
b: Elilim sounds like elohim, "gods," but comes from a word meaning "weak, worthless." Isaiah loves the word (Isaiah 2:8, 18, 20; 10:10–11), and Psalm 96:5 makes the pun plain: "Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god," setting elohim beside elilim. "Gods out of poured metal" recalls the golden calf, "a calf of cast metal" in Exodus 32:4, where the Hebrew word is the same, massekah.

a: rotten meat
p: Piggul is meat gone foul. In rabbinic law it is a technical term for a spoiled sacrifice.
b: Piggul appears only four times in the Bible (7:18; 19:7; Isaiah 65:4; Ezekiel 4:14), always of unclean, stinking meat. In a hot climate, sacrificial meat left until the third day would be spoiling. The rabbis made piggul a legal category: a sacrifice offered with the intention of eating it at the wrong time becomes invalid, and eating it brings the penalty of being cut off (Mishnah Zevachim 2:2–3). The rule also kept the peace offering a shared meal, eaten quickly with family and the poor, not stored.

a: do not harvest all the way to the edge of your field
t: Peah: the corner of the field
p: The rabbis gave a whole tractate to this law. It is the background of the book of Ruth.
b: The edge, pe'ah, and the gleanings, leqet, belong to the poor. The Mishnah tractate Pe'ah sets the edge at no less than one sixtieth of the field, and opens: "These are things that have no fixed measure: the corner of the field, the first fruits, the pilgrimage offering, acts of kindness and the study of Torah." The law is not charity handed down but a right of the poor to gather for themselves, with dignity. Ruth gleaning behind Boaz's reapers shows how it worked (Ruth 2). The law is repeated in the feast calendar (23:22), tying worship to justice.

a: Do not steal.
p: Many of the Ten Commandments return here, applied to daily life.
b: "Do not steal" repeats the Eighth Commandment (Exodus 20:15), and the verses around it widen it: do not deceive, do not deal falsely (19:11), do not swear falsely (19:12), do not hold back wages (19:13). The rabbis read "do not steal" here as covering theft of property, and the commandment in Exodus as covering kidnapping, "stealing a person" (Talmud, Sanhedrin 86a). The chapter keeps turning the big commands into specific habits.

a: Do not swear by my name to a lie
p: An oath calls God as witness. Jesus builds on this verse in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: Swearing "by my name to a lie" makes God a witness to something false, and so treats his name as common. The verse joins the Third Commandment, about lifting up the LORD's name for nothing (Exodus 20:7), with the ban on false witness. Numbers 30:2 adds that a man who swears must not break his word. Jesus cites the teaching, "You must not swear falsely, but you must pay to the Lord what you promised under oath" (Matthew 5:33), and goes further: do not swear at all, but let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:34–37; James 5:12). Quakers and some Anabaptists refuse oaths in court for this reason; most Christians allow them.
r: Exodus 20:7; Exodus 20:16; Numbers 30:2; Zechariah 5:4; Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12

a: The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight until morning.
p: Day laborers lived hand to mouth. Holding their pay overnight is a sin in the law and the prophets.
b: Deuteronomy explains: pay him each day before the sun goes down, "because he is poor and his heart is set on it" (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Jeremiah condemns the king who "has his fellow citizen work for nothing" (Jeremiah 22:13), and Malachi lists those "who squeeze the hired worker out of his pay" with sorcerers and adulterers (Malachi 3:5). James warns the rich: "The pay of the laborers who cut your fields, the pay you cheated them out of, cries out" (James 5:4). In Jesus' parable, the landowner pays his workers at evening (Matthew 20:8). Jewish law still requires prompt payment of wages (bal talin).

a: do not set something to trip over in front of a blind person
p: The rabbis read this law as forbidding bad advice and helping others to sin. Paul uses the same image.
b: The literal law protects the disabled: do not curse the deaf, who cannot hear you, or trip the blind, who cannot see you. "Fear your God" follows, because God sees what the victim cannot. The rabbis widened lifnei 'iver, "before the blind": do not give someone advice that harms him, and do not help someone sin, such as offering wine to a Nazirite or lending at interest (Sifra; Talmud, Pesachim 22b; Avodah Zarah 6a–b). Paul tells the Romans not to put "a stumbling block" in a fellow believer's way (Romans 14:13), and Jesus warns against causing "little ones" to stumble (Matthew 18:6).

a: Do not lift up the face of the poor man, and do not honor the face of the great man
p: To "lift someone's face" is to show him favor. Justice favors neither rich nor poor.
b: In Hebrew, to "lift up the face" of someone (nasa panim) is to accept him, to favor him; to "honor the face" is to defer to someone important. The law forbids both. Exodus already warns against favoring the poor in court (Exodus 23:3). Judges must not tilt toward the poor out of pity, nor toward the powerful out of fear: "in what is right you will judge." The New Testament word for favoritism, prosōpolēmpsia, "face-taking," is built on this idiom (James 2:1, 9; Romans 2:11).
r: Exodus 23:3, 6; Deuteronomy 1:17; Deuteronomy 16:19; James 2:1–9; Romans 2:11; Acts 10:34

a: Do not stand by over your neighbor's blood
p: The Hebrew is unclear. The rabbis read it as a duty to rescue.
b: Literally, "Do not stand on your neighbor's blood." The rabbis read it, "Do not stand idly by when your neighbor's life is in danger": if you see someone drowning or attacked by robbers, you must help (Sifra; Talmud, Sanhedrin 73a). Other readers, noting the slander in the first half of the verse, take it as "do not stand up against your neighbor's life," that is, do not testify falsely to get him killed, as at Naboth's trial (1 Kings 21:10–13). Some take it as "do not profit from his blood." The Plain text keeps a phrase as open as the Hebrew. Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan presses the rescue reading (Luke 10:30–37).
orig: לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל־דַּם רֵעֶךָ (lo ta'amod 'al-dam re'ekha)

a: Be sure to correct your fellow citizen
t: Correct him rather than hate him
p: Speaking up is the cure for secret hatred. Qumran and Jesus both built rules on this verse.
b: The verse sets hidden hatred against open correction: say it to his face, and you will not "carry sin because of him," either the sin of hating him or a share in his wrongdoing. The Dead Sea community made it a procedure: a member must correct a brother the same day, before witnesses, and not hold the matter in anger (Damascus Document 9:2–8; Community Rule 5:24–6:1). Jesus gives a similar order: "go and correct him, with just the two of you there" (Matthew 18:15), and "If your brother sins, take him to task, and if he repents, forgive him" (Luke 17:3). The Talmud asks whether anyone in its day still knew how to correct well (Arakhin 16b).
orig: הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ (hokheach tokhiach), "you shall surely correct"

a: You are to love your neighbor as yourself.
t: Love your neighbor: Hillel, Akiva and Jesus
p: The most quoted verse of Leviticus. Rabbis and Jesus both called it a summary of the law.
b: This is the most quoted line of Leviticus. Rabbi Akiva called it "a great principle of the Torah" (Sifra), and Jesus named it the second great commandment (Mark 12:31), also listing it for the rich young man (Matthew 19:19). In context it answers the first half of the verse: instead of taking revenge or nursing a grudge, act for your neighbor's good. For Hillel, Ben Azzai, Jesus, Paul and James on this verse, see the chapter page, "Love your neighbor: from Hillel to Paul."
r: 19:34; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 19:19; Matthew 22:36–40; Luke 10:25–28; Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8

a: your neighbor
p: In context the re'a is a fellow Israelite. Leviticus itself widens love to the foreigner in 19:34.
b: Re'a means a companion, fellow or neighbor. In the verse it stands parallel to "the children of your people," so the first circle is fellow Israelites. But 19:34 uses the very same words for the foreigner: "you are to love him as yourself." When a lawyer asked Jesus "Who is my neighbor?" he answered with a Samaritan who acted as one (Luke 10:29–37). Jesus also quoted a saying, "Love your neighbor and hate your enemy" (Matthew 5:43); the second half is not in Leviticus, but the Dead Sea Community Rule tells members to "hate all the sons of darkness" (Community Rule, column 1, line 10). Jesus answers, "Love your enemies."

a: as yourself
p: Hebrew grammar allows a second reading: love your neighbor, for he is like you.
b: The usual reading is "love your neighbor as you love yourself." But the verb here takes an unusual preposition, "love to your neighbor" (ve'ahavta lere'akha), found also in 19:34, and kamokha can mean "one like you." The Jewish thinker Naphtali Herz Wessely and later Martin Buber read it as "love your neighbor: he is like you," a person with the same needs and dignity. Some scholars, noting the preposition, take "love" here as practical kindness: do good to your neighbor. The Greek translation, which Jesus and Paul quote, reads hōs seauton, "as yourself." The Plain text follows that reading, held by most interpreters, and leaves the alternative here.

a: Do not let a garment of two kinds of thread woven together come upon your body
p: Shatnez, wool woven with linen, was the mix used in priestly clothing. Many think that is the point.
b: The rare word sha'atnez is explained in Deuteronomy 22:11 as wool and linen together. Observant Jews still have clothing tested for shatnez. Why forbid it? The tabernacle curtains and the high priest's sash were woven of linen with dyed wool (Exodus 26:1; 39:29), and Josephus says the mixture was reserved for priests (Antiquities 4.208). Jacob Milgrom argued that mixtures belong to the holy sphere, so lay people may not copy them. Mary Douglas read all three bans as acting out the creation order, "each by its kind" (Genesis 1:11–25). Others suspect links to foreign magic, or simply see laws whose reason God did not give, which the rabbis called chuqqim.

a: damages are due
p: The rare word bikkoret has been read three ways, and the verse is hard in every reading.
b: Bikkoret appears only here. The KJV, following the rabbis, read "she shall be scourged" (Mishnah Keritot 2:4 says the woman is flogged). Many modern translations have "there must be an inquiry" or "due punishment." Others, comparing an Akkadian word for a claim, read "there shall be compensation" paid to the man she was promised to (Jacob Milgrom, following E. A. Speiser). The point is that the case is not adultery, since a slave woman not yet freed was not legally a wife, so there is no death penalty (compare 20:10); the man brings a guilt offering instead. Modern readers often note that the woman, a slave, has no voice in the law at all.

a: count its fruit as its foreskin
p: A young tree's fruit is "uncircumcised" for three years. Jewish farmers still keep the rule of orlah.
b: The image is bold: the first fruit is like a foreskin, not yet given to God. The same word is used of uncircumcised lips (Exodus 6:12), ears (Jeremiah 6:10) and hearts (26:41). Jewish law keeps the rule of 'orlah: fruit from a tree's first three years may not be eaten, and the fourth year's fruit (neta' revai) was eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed. Horticulturists note that removing early fruit strengthens a young tree, which fits 19:25, "so that it will yield you more."

a: Do not eat anything with the blood.
p: Hebrew 'al haddam can mean eating meat with its blood, or eating beside blood poured out for spirits.
b: 'Al haddam usually means "with the blood," repeating 17:10–14 (as in 1 Samuel 14:32–33). But it can also mean "over the blood," and the verse goes straight on to omens and signs. Maimonides thought some pagans ate beside a pit of blood to commune with spirits (Guide 3.46), and some modern scholars agree. The rabbis drew from the verse a ban on eating before praying for one's life, and on a court eating on the day it executes someone (Talmud, Sanhedrin 63a).

a: Do not look for omens, and do not read signs.
p: Israel's neighbors read the future in livers, stars, birds and smoke. Leviticus forbids it.
b: Nichesh (look for omens) is what Joseph's servant claims his master does with his cup (Genesis 44:5); 'onen (read signs) may relate to clouds or to a hum or murmur. Mesopotamia produced huge omen collections, reading sheep livers, the flight of birds and the stars. Deuteronomy 18:10–14 gives the fullest list of banned practices and says God will send a prophet instead (Deuteronomy 18:15). Balaam says, "no omen works against Jacob" (Numbers 23:23).

a: Do not cut your hair round at the sides of your head
p: From this verse come the side curls worn by many Orthodox and Hasidic Jewish men.
b: The "sides" (pe'ot) of the head are the hair at the temples. Herodotus says some Arabs cut their hair round, shaved at the temples, in honor of their god (Histories 3.8), and Jeremiah mentions desert peoples "who clip the edges of their hair" (Jeremiah 9:26; 25:23). Jewish law forbids shaving the temples bald, and many Orthodox, Hasidic and Yemenite Jewish men leave long side curls (peyot). The beard law forbids shaving with a blade, so many observant men use scissors or electric shavers. Priests had the same rules, with mourning added (21:5).

a: do not put tattooed writing on yourselves
p: The phrase means "writing of an incision." Jewish law forbids tattoos; Christians differ.
b: Ketovet qa'aqa', "writing of a cut," appears only here. It probably means marks cut or pricked into the skin and filled with ink, perhaps in mourning, since the first half forbids gashing the body "for someone who has died." Slashing oneself was a pagan mourning rite and a way to rouse a god (1 Kings 18:28; Jeremiah 16:6; 41:5). Jewish law forbids tattoos (Mishnah Makkot 3:6), though it does not bar a tattooed Jew from burial, as is often said. Christians divide: some apply the verse today, while many read it as part of the ritual law. Isaiah 44:5 pictures people writing "the LORD's" on their hands.

a: Do not make your daughter common by turning her into a prostitute
p: Poverty pushed some fathers to sell daughters into prostitution. The law forbids it.
b: A father who made money from his daughter's body would "make her common," the same word used for profaning holy things. Some scholars think of sacred prostitution at shrines, though whether it existed in the ancient Near East is now widely doubted. Most see ordinary poverty: Exodus 21:7 lets a father sell a daughter as a servant-wife, but not this. The land itself is again pictured as a body that can be defiled (18:25), and the result is zimmah, "vile schemes" (18:17).

a: the ghosts of the dead or to the spirits that know things
p: These words can mean the spirits of the dead themselves, or the people who call them up.
b: Ov may originally mean a pit in the ground, through which the dead were called up: a Hittite word for a ritual pit, a-a-pi, is close (Harry Hoffner). The woman at Endor is "mistress of an ov" and brings up Samuel's ghost (1 Samuel 28:7–19). Yidde'oni, from the verb "know," is "the knowing one," a spirit (or person) who knows the future. Isaiah mocks those who consult "the ghosts that twitter and murmur" instead of God (Isaiah 8:19). The KJV's "familiar spirits" and "wizards" reflect a later world. In 20:27 the words are used of the people "in whom" a ghost is.

a: Rise up before gray hair
p: Jewish law still requires standing for the elderly and for scholars.
b: The Talmud asks whether "the old" means any elderly person or a learned one, and concludes that one rises for both, even for an old person who is not learned (Kiddushin 32b–33a). Proverbs calls gray hair "a crown of beauty" (Proverbs 16:31), and the honor shown the old is placed next to "fear your God," as in 19:14: God sees whether we honor those who cannot demand it. Job 32:6 shows the same custom: the young Elihu waits for the old to speak first.

a: You are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
p: The same words as 19:18, now for the outsider. Israel's own past in Egypt is the reason.
b: Exodus told Israel not to oppress the foreigner, "for you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21; 23:9). Leviticus goes further: love him as yourself. Deuteronomy says God himself "loves the foreigner" (Deuteronomy 10:18–19). The Septuagint translates ger here as prosēlytos, "one who has come over," and the rabbis usually read the law of the convert to Judaism (ger tzedek), while modern scholars mostly see a resident non-Israelite. The Talmud counts that the Torah warns against wronging the ger thirty-six times, some say forty-six (Bava Metzia 59b). Modern refugee and immigration debates often cite this verse.

a: an ephah that is right and a hin that is right
p: Merchants cheated with two sets of weights. Archaeologists have found weights that do not match.
b: An ephah was a dry measure of about two thirds of a bushel; a hin a liquid measure of about a gallon. Traders could keep a heavy weight for buying and a light one for selling (Deuteronomy 25:13–16). Inscribed stone weights from Judah, marked in shekels, vary noticeably from one another, which shows why the law insisted. Amos accuses merchants who say, "We will make the ephah small and the shekel large" (Amos 8:5), and Proverbs says false scales are "abhorrent to the LORD" (Proverbs 11:1). The verse ends by naming the exodus: the God who freed slaves cares about the grocer's scale.
r: Deuteronomy 25:13–16; Amos 8:4–6; Micah 6:10–11; Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 20:10; Ezekiel 45:10

a: must be put to death
p: Chapter 18 forbids; chapter 20 sets penalties. The two read like a law and its sentencing table.
b: Most of the acts banned in chapter 18 return here, now with penalties: death by the community, being cut off by God, or childlessness. Scholars note that chapter 20 is arranged by penalty, not by relative, and that it adds a few items (cursing parents, ghosts). The repeated phrase mot yumat, "he shall surely be put to death," is the language of Israel's oldest law (Exodus 21:12–17). Ancient law collections, such as Hammurabi's, often gave a rule and its penalty together; Leviticus separates them, and frames both with calls to holiness (20:7–8, 22–26). Ezekiel 22:9–11 lists many of the same sins, almost in this order, among the reasons for Jerusalem's fall.
orig: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat), "dying he will be put to death"

a: The people of the land are to stone him with stones.
p: Stoning was carried out by the whole community, outside the camp or city.
b: Stoning made the whole people responsible for the sentence (24:14; Deuteronomy 17:7: "The hands of the witnesses are to be first against him"). "The people of the land" here means the ordinary citizens. The Mishnah describes the procedure in detail: the condemned man was pushed from a height twice a man's size, and if he still lived a witness dropped a stone on him; only if he still lived did all the people throw (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4). In the New Testament, Stephen was stoned outside Jerusalem (Acts 7:58), and crowds tried to stone Jesus (John 8:59; 10:31).

a: and so made my holy place unclean
t: Polluting the sanctuary from far away
p: A sin committed at home pollutes God's sanctuary. This is a key idea in Milgrom's reading of Leviticus.
b: The Molech worshiper did not enter the tent of meeting, yet he "made my holy place unclean." Jacob Milgrom built his reading of the purification offering on such verses: Israel's sins pollute the sanctuary from a distance, like a magnet drawing dust, and the sanctuary must be cleansed every year on the Day of Atonement (16:16). If the pollution grows too great, God leaves, as Ezekiel saw (Ezekiel 8–11). Others read the phrase more simply: worshiping Molech at the LORD's own festivals or in his name defiles his sanctuary (compare Ezekiel 23:38–39, where child sacrifice and Temple worship happen on the same day).

a: and against his clan
p: The guilty man's clan, and a community that looks away, share the blame.
b: If the people "look the other way" (20:4), God himself acts, against the man "and against his clan." The rabbis worried about punishing relatives and explained: the family that covered for him shares his guilt, though not his penalty (Sifra). Many readers hear a principle about complicity: a society that ignores the sacrifice of children is not innocent. Ezekiel 18 insists that each person dies for his own sin, which some see as a correction of the idea of family guilt and others as a different setting.

a: his blood is on him
p: A legal formula: his death is his own fault, and those who carry out the sentence are not guilty.
b: Damav bo, "his bloods are on him," clears the executioners: the condemned man brought his death on himself, so no blood guilt falls on the community (compare Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16). The rabbis noted that the formula appears with stoning in 20:27 and concluded that every case marked "their blood is on them" was punished by stoning (Talmud, Sanhedrin 54a). Matthew's crowd says, "His blood on us, and on our children!" (Matthew 27:25), using the same idiom to accept responsibility, a verse with a tragic history of being used against Jews.

a: Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death.
p: Jesus quotes this law against those who used religious gifts to dodge caring for parents.
b: The law repeats Exodus: "Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death" (Exodus 21:17). Jesus quotes it in Mark 7:10 and Matthew 15:4 against the practice of declaring one's property korban, a gift to God, so it could not be used to support one's parents. To "curse" (qillel) is literally to treat as light, the opposite of "honor," which means to treat as heavy. The rabbis limited the death penalty to cursing parents with God's name (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:8).

a: A man who commits adultery with another man's wife, who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife
p: The repeated words may be a copying slip. The law stands behind the story of the woman brought to Jesus.
b: The clause "who commits adultery" appears twice; many scholars think a scribe copied it twice by accident, though others read the second as an explanation. The law punishes both partners (Deuteronomy 22:22). In John 7:53–8:11 the scribes bring Jesus a woman caught in adultery: "In the law Moses ordered us to stone women like this." Jesus answers, "The one among you who is without sin should be the first to throw a stone at her." That passage is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts and was probably added later, though many think it preserves a true story. Notice that only the woman was brought, though the law names both. The Mishnah prescribes strangling for a married adulteress, stoning only for a betrothed one (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4; 11:1).

a: They have done a wrongful mixing.
p: Judah unknowingly broke this law with Tamar. The Bible tells it without a death sentence.
b: Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law, disguised herself, and Judah slept with her (Genesis 38). Judah first ordered her burned, then confessed, "She is more in the right than I" (Genesis 38:26). Their son Perez became the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–22) and appears in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:3). The rabbis said Judah was not guilty because he did not know who she was. The story is often read as evidence of a time before these laws, or of how Scripture lets grace and law stand side by side.

a: the two of them have done something abhorrent
p: Unlike 18:22, this verse names both partners and a penalty. How readers apply it varies widely.
b: Leviticus 20:13 adds what 18:22 lacks: both men are guilty, and the sentence is death. Saul Olyan thinks the words "the two of them" were added later to a law first aimed at the active partner; most scholars read the verse as it stands. In rabbinic law the penalty required two witnesses who had warned the men beforehand, which made it nearly impossible to carry out (see 20:27). Medieval and early modern Christian states applied it: the Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) cited this verse for its capital law. Today almost all Jews and Christians who keep 18:22 as moral teaching reject the death penalty for it, because they see the civil penalties as belonging to ancient Israel (Westminster Confession 19.4) or to the Sanhedrin. A small Christian movement called theonomy (Greg Bahnsen) argued for keeping the penalties.

a: They are to burn him and them in fire
p: Who is burned, and how? Both questions divided the rabbis.
b: Burning is the penalty here and for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute (21:9); Judah once ordered it for Tamar (Genesis 38:24). "Him and them" sounds as if both women die, even the wife who may have been innocent. The rabbis read it as "him and one of them," the mother-in-law (Talmud, Sanhedrin 76b). They also explained burning as pouring molten lead down the throat, so the body was not consumed (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:2), while some modern scholars think the body was burned after death. Joshua 7:25 shows a body burned after stoning.

a: you are to kill the animal
p: The animal is not guilty. Readers give several reasons for its death.
b: An animal cannot sin, so why kill it? The Mishnah answers: so that it will not walk through the market and people say, "That is the one for whom so-and-so was stoned" (Sanhedrin 7:4). Others point to the ox that kills a person, which is also stoned (Exodus 21:28), and see the animal as polluted by the act. Mary Douglas and others read it as removing a living confusion of kinds (18:23).

a: it is a disgrace
t: Chesed: a word with two faces
p: The word for "disgrace" is spelled like chesed, "loyal love." It is a separate, rare word.
b: Usually chesed means steadfast love, the great covenant word. Here, and in Proverbs 14:34 ("but sin brings peoples shame," where "shame" is chesed), it means shame, disgrace. Most scholars think these are two different words that happen to look alike, as in Aramaic where the root means "to reproach." The rabbis played on the coincidence: Cain married his sister by God's "kindness," since the first family had no one else (Sanhedrin 58b). "Seeing nakedness" here is plain language for sex, as "exposing" is elsewhere.

a: has laid bare her fountain
p: Menstrual blood is called a fountain or spring. Life and death meet in it.
b: The word maqor, "spring, fountain," is used of God as "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13) and of a wife as the husband's "fountain" (Proverbs 5:18). Blood is life (17:11), and the loss of it in menstruation was treated as a contact with death, which is why it made a person unclean (15:19). For how this verse fits 15:24, see the note on 18:19.

a: They will be childless.
p: Henry VIII used this verse to argue his marriage to his brother's widow was void.
b: Catherine of Aragon had married Henry's older brother Arthur, who died. Pope Julius II granted a dispensation, and Henry married her. When no son survived, Henry cited this verse: "They will be childless." He argued that no pope could set aside God's law, so the marriage had never been valid. Catherine's side pointed to Deuteronomy 25:5, which commands marriage to a dead brother's wife, and said Leviticus forbids it only while the brother lives. The dispute helped trigger England's break with Rome in the 1530s. The rabbis discussed whether "childless" means that no children would be born, or that they would die young.
l: Annulment of the marriage of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon

a: So you must set apart the clean animal from the unclean
t: Food laws and a separated people
p: The food laws are tied directly to Israel's separation from the nations. Acts 10 untied them.
b: God "set you apart from the peoples" (20:24), so Israel must "set apart" clean from unclean animals (chapter 11). The same verb, hivdil, is used of God separating light from darkness at creation (Genesis 1:4). Mary Douglas argued that the menu mirrors the people: as Israel is set apart from the nations, so clean animals are set apart from unclean, and eating becomes a daily reminder of election. In Acts 10 Peter sees unclean animals in a vision and hears "do not call common what God has made clean"; he understands it as being about Gentile people (Acts 10:28). Jewish tradition keeps kashrut as a living sign of the covenant.

a: must be put to death
t: Did Israel carry out these sentences?
p: Rabbinic law set up rules that made execution very rare. Some later Christian states revived the penalties.
b: The Bible records few executions under these laws: the blasphemer (24:23), the Sabbath breaker (Numbers 15:36), Achan (Joshua 7). Rabbinic law required two eyewitnesses, a warning just before the act, and a court of twenty-three. The Mishnah records a debate. A court that executed once in seven years was called "destructive"; Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah said once in seventy; Rabbis Tarfon and Akiva said that on their court no one would ever have been put to death; and Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel replied that they would have multiplied murderers in Israel (Mishnah Makkot 1:10). The rabbis also held that a court could punish beyond the letter of the law in a crisis, as when Simeon ben Shetach hanged eighty women at Ashkelon (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4; Talmud, Sanhedrin 46a). John 18:31 says the council could not execute under Rome; historians debate how far that was true.

a: A priest must not make himself unclean for a dead person
p: Death was the strongest source of uncleanness. Priests had to keep away from it.
b: Touching a corpse, or being under the same roof with one, made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–16). Since priests served the living God at the altar, they could join a funeral only for close blood relatives. Many scholars contrast this with Egypt, where priests cared for the dead and the cult of the dead was central; Israel's priests stand on the side of life. Ezekiel's temple vision repeats the rule (Ezekiel 44:25), and Jesus' parable has a priest pass by a man left "half dead" (Luke 10:31), perhaps fearing that very uncleanness.

a: for his mother and his father
p: The list of close relatives does not name the priest's wife. The rabbis said she is included.
b: Mother, father, son, daughter, brother, unmarried sister: the wife is missing. The rabbis read "his relative who is near to him" (she'ero) at the start of 21:2 as meaning his wife, and Jewish law requires a priest to bury his wife (Sifra; Talmud, Yevamot 22b). Others read the obscure 21:4 as forbidding a priest to defile himself even for his wife. Ezekiel, a priest, is told not to mourn publicly when his wife dies (Ezekiel 24:15–18), which suggests he would normally have done so.

a: as a husband among his kin
p: Ba'al can mean husband, master or chief. Each meaning gives a different law.
b: The Hebrew reads, "He shall not make himself unclean, a ba'al among his people, to make himself common." If ba'al means "husband," a priest may not defile himself for relatives by marriage, his in-laws (BSB), or for his wife. If it means "chief, leader," the priest is a leading man who must not become unclean at all for outsiders (KJV). Some scholars change one letter to read "for a married woman," meaning a sister who has married out of the family. The Plain text keeps the most literal sense and leaves the meaning open.

a: the food of their God
p: The offerings are called God's lechem, "bread, food." Did Israel think God ate?
b: "The food of their God" (lechem eloheihem) appears often in these chapters (21:6, 8, 17, 21, 22; 22:25). In Babylon and Egypt, gods were fed meals twice a day before their statues. Leviticus keeps the old phrase, but the offering goes up in smoke and the meat is eaten by priests and worshipers. Psalm 50:12–13 mocks the idea: "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you... Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls?" Malachi 1:7 uses "food" for the altar offerings, and the KJV's "bread of their God" is literal.

a: who has been made common
p: A woman "made common": one violated, or of a priest's forbidden union.
b: Chalalah comes from the verb "make common, profane." Some read it with "prostitute" as "a prostitute and defiled woman," one person. The rabbis made it a legal category: a woman born of, or involved in, a union forbidden to a priest, such as a divorcée who married a priest, or the daughter of such a marriage. Others think of a woman who was raped. Jewish law still forbids a kohen, a man of priestly descent, to marry a divorced woman or a convert, and the Israeli rabbinate, which controls Jewish marriage there, will not perform such a marriage.

a: You are to treat him as holy
p: The command shifts to the people: treat the priest as holy. The rabbis applied it to Kohanim today.
b: The verse suddenly turns from the priests to Israel: "you" must make him holy. Jewish law still honors a kohen: he is called first to the Torah reading and leads grace after meals when present (Talmud, Gittin 59b; Nedarim 62a). In synagogue the Kohanim bless the people with the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. The change from "him" to "you" to "I" in the verse is typical of the Holiness Code's way of tying everyone into God's holiness.

a: She is to be burned in fire.
p: The harshest penalty falls on a priest's daughter. Readers note what it says about holiness and about women.
b: A priest's household shares his holiness (22:11–13), so his daughter's prostitution "makes her father common." The penalty is burning, as in 20:14. The rabbis limited the law to a married or betrothed daughter who commits adultery (Talmud, Sanhedrin 50b–51a) and described burning as molten lead (see 20:14). Feminist readers have pointed out that the law punishes the daughter for her father's honor and names no man involved. Traditional readers see the weight of holiness: the closer to God, the higher the standard (10:3).

a: must not let his hair hang loose or tear his clothes
t: The high priest tears his robe
p: The high priest may not tear his clothes. At Jesus' trial, Caiaphas does.
b: Letting the hair loose and tearing one's clothes were signs of mourning (10:6; Genesis 37:34). The high priest may never do them. Yet at Jesus' trial, "the high priest tore his clothes" and said, "He has blasphemed" (Matthew 26:65; Mark 14:63). The rabbis allowed tearing at hearing blasphemy, only at the bottom of the garment, and read this verse as forbidding the mourning tear (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5; Mishnah Horayot 3:5). Christian writers since the church fathers have seen Caiaphas tearing his robe as a sign that the old priesthood was ending (Hebrews 7:11–12).

a: the crown of his God's anointing oil is on him
p: Nezer is the word for the high priest's gold plate, a king's crown, and a Nazirite's vow.
b: Nezer means something set apart: the gold plate on the high priest's turban is "the holy crown" (Exodus 29:6; 39:30), a king's crown is a nezer (2 Samuel 1:10), and a Nazirite's uncut hair is "the nezer of his God" on his head (Numbers 6:7). The anointing oil marks the high priest as wholly God's, so he may not leave the sanctuary even to follow a parent's body. The KJV keeps "crown"; many modern versions have "consecration."

a: Only a virgin from his own kin may he take as his wife
p: Christian writers read this as a picture of Christ and the church. Ezekiel loosened it for ordinary priests.
b: The high priest must marry a virgin "from his own kin," probably meaning from Israel (some say from priestly families). Ezekiel's temple law lets ordinary priests marry a virgin of Israel or a priest's widow (Ezekiel 44:22). Christian interpreters, starting from Paul's picture of Christ presenting the church as "a pure virgin" (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25–27), read the rule as a type, a pattern pointing to Christ the high priest. Jewish readers note simply that the high priest, alone, must keep his line wholly within Israel's holiness.

a: who has a defect
p: Disabled priests could not serve at the altar, but they remained priests and ate the holy food.
b: The word mum, "defect, blemish," is the same used of animals unfit for sacrifice (22:20–25). A priest with a defect could not offer sacrifices or enter beyond the curtain, but he was still a priest and ate the most holy food (21:22). Ancient readers saw a matter of visible wholeness before God, as with the animals; Mary Douglas tied it to the idea that holiness means wholeness. Modern readers, especially in disability theology, find the rule painful and point to Jesus, who healed "the blind and the lame" who came to him in the Temple (Matthew 21:14), and to Isaiah's promise that the lame will leap (Isaiah 35:6). The Dead Sea community barred people with such defects from its assembly (1QSa 2:3–9).

a: a slit nose or a limb too long
p: Several of these terms are rare, and their meanings are guesses.
b: Charum may mean a split or flattened nose (KJV "flat nose"), or more generally someone disfigured. Sarua' means "stretched out," perhaps a limb too long or a deformity. In 21:20 daq means "thin" (a dwarf, or someone withered), tevallul be'eino is "a mixture in his eye," perhaps a white spot or cataract, and garav and yallefet are skin diseases. The Mishnah gives long lists of blemishes that disqualify priests and animals (Bekhorot 6–7).

a: he must not go in to the curtain
p: Hebrews calls Christ a high priest "holy, innocent, undefiled," who went beyond the curtain.
b: The curtain separated the holy place from the most holy place (Exodus 26:31–33). Hebrews speaks of Jesus as "the high priest that suited us: holy, free of evil, free of stain, separated from sinners" (Hebrews 7:26), who went "in to the inner side of the veil" for us (Hebrews 6:19–20) and "offered himself flawless to God" (Hebrews 9:14). At his death "the sanctuary curtain was torn in two from the top down to the bottom" (Mark 15:38). For Christian readers these rules about wholeness are fulfilled in one priest, and the way into God's presence is opened to all who come through him (Hebrews 10:19–22).
r: 16:2; Exodus 26:31–33; Hebrews 6:19–20; Hebrews 7:26; Hebrews 9:14; Hebrews 10:19–22; Mark 15:38

a: to keep themselves apart from the holy gifts
p: The verb nazar, "keep apart," is the root of Nazirite.
b: Vayinnazru means "let them hold themselves apart" or "be careful with." It comes from the root of nazir, the Nazirite who is set apart (Numbers 6:2). The holy gifts (qodashim) are the parts of offerings that belong to priests. Priests ate them, but only when ritually clean; the chapter lists what makes them unfit and who may share their table. The point is that holy food is not common food, even for those whose living depends on it.

a: a skin disease
p: The skin disease of Leviticus 13–14 is not the disease now called leprosy.
b: Tsara'at (KJV "leper") covers flaky, scaly skin conditions, and also mold on cloth and walls (13:47–59; 14:33–53). Hansen's disease, modern leprosy, does not match the symptoms described and may not have reached the Near East until later. See chapters 13–14. Here the point is that a priest with any such condition must wait until he is declared clean before eating holy food.

a: No outsider may eat a holy gift.
t: Who belongs to the priest's household
p: A slave bought or born in the house may eat holy food. A paid lodger or worker may not.
b: Zar, "outsider," means anyone outside the priest's family. The law draws the line in an unexpected place: a hired worker or a lodger, though free, is an outsider, but a slave bought with the priest's money, or born in his house, is part of the household and eats with it (22:11). The same logic governs who may eat the Passover: a bought slave who is circumcised may eat, a lodger or hired worker may not (Exodus 12:43–45). Modern readers find slavery troubling here; the law's own concern is belonging, not status. A married daughter leaves the household, and a widowed or divorced one without children returns to it (22:12–13).

a: he must add a fifth to it
p: Repayment plus twenty percent, the same rule as the guilt offering.
b: Someone who eats a priest's food by mistake must replace it and add a fifth, like the man who misuses holy property in 5:16. The rabbis explained that the fifth is counted so that the added fifth is a fifth of the total, that is, a quarter of the original (Talmud, Bava Metzia 54a). The principle of restitution plus a penalty appears also in theft laws (6:5; Numbers 5:7) and in Zacchaeus's promise to pay back fourfold (Luke 19:8).

a: a flawless male
p: The animal must be tamim, "whole." The same word describes Noah and Abraham.
b: Tamim means complete, whole, without flaw. It describes sacrificial animals (1:3; Exodus 12:5) and people of integrity: Noah was "blameless" (tamim) in his generations (Genesis 6:9), and Abraham was told, "Go about your life in my sight, and be whole" (Genesis 17:1). The New Testament calls Christ "a lamb with no flaw and no stain" (1 Peter 1:19) and calls the church to be "holy and faultless" (Ephesians 5:27). The KJV has "without blemish" and in 22:21 "perfect"; the Plain text uses "flawless" throughout Leviticus.

a: Do not present to the LORD anything blind, or injured
p: Centuries later Malachi accuses the priests of offering exactly these animals.
b: "You bring a blind animal to sacrifice. Is that not evil? You bring one that is lame or sick. Is that not evil? Go ahead, bring it to your governor. Will he accept you?" (Malachi 1:8). Malachi says a cheat who vows a good male and gives a damaged one is cursed (Malachi 1:13–14). The law of the sound animal is about giving God one's best, not one's leftovers, a theme Christians apply to giving and service (Romans 12:1).

a: you may offer as a freewill gift
p: A freewill gift is given unasked; a vow repays a promise. The vow demands a better animal.
b: A nedavah, "freewill gift," is given spontaneously, as when the people brought materials for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:29). A neder, "vow," is a promise made in need, such as Jacob's promise at Bethel, made on condition that God would guard him on the road (Genesis 28:20–22; 1 Samuel 1:11). Because a vow is a debt, a lesser animal will not do. For vows of persons and property, see chapter 27.

a: Do not do this in your land.
p: The rabbis read "do not do this in your land" as forbidding castration of any animal, or person.
b: The verse could mean only "do not offer such animals in your land." But the rabbis read it as a separate law: do not castrate any male, animal or human (Sifra; Talmud, Shabbat 110b–111a). Jewish law still forbids it, so Jewish farmers did not geld animals. Deuteronomy 23:1 excludes a castrated man from the assembly, but Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs who keep the covenant "a name that is better than sons and daughters," and in Acts 8:26–39 an Ethiopian eunuch is one of the first non-Jews baptized.

a: from the hand of a foreigner
p: Foreigners, not only resident ones, could send offerings to Israel's God.
b: Ben nekhar is a true foreigner, not the resident ger. The verse assumes such people may bring sacrifices, as long as the animals are sound. Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes to pray at the Temple (1 Kings 8:41–43), and in the Second Temple era foreign rulers sent offerings; Josephus says the refusal to accept sacrifices for the Roman emperor in AD 66 started the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.409–410). The rabbis allowed Gentiles to offer burnt offerings but not other kinds.

a: it is to stay seven days with its mother
p: Like a boy's circumcision, an animal's offering waits until the eighth day.
b: Exodus gave the same rule for firstborn animals: seven days with the mother, given to God on the eighth (Exodus 22:30). Boys were circumcised on the eighth day (12:3; Genesis 17:12), and priests began serving on the eighth day after their ordination (9:1). Seven days completes a full cycle of life, like creation's week, before the newborn enters God's service. The rabbis also saw kindness to the mother animal here.

a: do not slaughter the mother and her young on one day
p: Is this law about compassion? The rabbis argued over it.
b: Maimonides said the reason is compassion: animals feel grief, and a mother animal suffers seeing her young killed (Guide 3.48). The Aramaic Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds a line: "My people, children of Israel, as I am merciful in heaven, so you shall be merciful on earth." But the Mishnah says a prayer leader who prays "Your mercy reaches the bird's nest" must be silenced, because God's laws are decrees, not only lessons in mercy (Mishnah Berakhot 5:3; Talmud, Berakhot 33b). Ramban answered that the laws teach us to be merciful. Similar laws: do not cook a kid in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19), and let the mother bird go (Deuteronomy 22:6–7).

a: so that I will be shown to be holy among the Israelites
p: From this verse the rabbis drew the duty to honor God's name, even by martyrdom.
b: "I will be shown holy among the Israelites" became the source of kiddush hashem, "sanctifying the Name": living so that God is honored, and, when forced in public to commit idolatry, murder or sexual sin, choosing death (Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a–b). Jewish martyrs from the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7) to the medieval massacres were remembered as dying "for the sanctification of the Name." Its opposite, chillul hashem, is any act that brings God's name into contempt. Jesus taught his followers to pray, "May your name be honored as holy" (Matthew 6:9), using the same idea.
orig: וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי (veniqdashti), "and I will be made holy"

a: These are the LORD's set times
p: The festivals are "appointed times," meetings God sets with his people.
