b: Mo'ed means a fixed time or meeting, from the verb "to appoint." The same root gives "tent of meeting" (ohel mo'ed): the festivals are meetings in time as the tent is a meeting in space. In Genesis 1:14 the lights in the sky mark "set times." "Holy gathering" (miqra' qodesh) literally means a holy calling or proclamation, a day called out as holy. The KJV's "feasts" is too narrow, since the list includes a fast day (23:27). Modern Hebrew still uses mo'adim for the festivals.

a: the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest
p: The weekly Sabbath comes first, before the yearly feasts.
b: "Sabbath of complete rest" (shabbat shabbaton), literally "a Sabbath of Sabbath-keeping," is used for the weekly Sabbath and for the Day of Atonement (23:32; 16:31). Placing the Sabbath first makes it the pattern for the whole calendar, which is built on sevens: the seventh day, seven weeks to the Feast of Weeks, the seventh month full of festivals, and in chapter 25 the seventh year and the Jubilee after seven times seven years. Some scholars think 23:2b–3 was added to an older list of yearly feasts, since 23:4 starts the list again.

a: between the two evenings
p: The Passover lamb was killed at dusk, or in the afternoon. Jewish groups disagreed which.
b: Bein ha'arbayim, "between the two evenings," is the time for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:6) and the evening offering (Exodus 29:39). The Samaritans and Karaites take it as between sunset and dark. The Pharisees and rabbis took it as the afternoon, from when the sun starts to decline (about 3 p.m.) to sunset, and Josephus says the lambs were killed from the ninth to the eleventh hour (Jewish War 6.423). That timing lies behind the Gospels' note that Jesus died at the ninth hour (Mark 15:34), when, in John's chronology, the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (John 19:14, 31).
r: Exodus 12:6; Exodus 29:39; Numbers 9:3; Deuteronomy 16:6; Mark 15:34; John 19:14

a: the LORD's Feast of Unleavened Bread
p: Two feasts in a row: the Passover meal on the 14th, then seven days of flat bread from the 15th.
b: Leviticus keeps Passover (the evening sacrifice) and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (a seven-day festival) distinct, as Exodus 12 does; later they were joined, and Jews today call the whole week Pesach. The rabbis' Seder meal, the removal of leaven and the eating of matzah all build on these verses and Exodus 12–13. Christians read Passover through the Last Supper and the cross: "our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered. So then, let us keep the feast ... but the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Easter's date is still tied to the Passover moon.
r: Exodus 12:1–20; Exodus 13:3–10; Numbers 28:16–25; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Luke 22:1, 7–20

a: Do no daily work.
p: Festival days ban "work of labor," a narrower ban than the Sabbath's "any work."
b: The Sabbath and the Day of Atonement forbid "any work" (kol melakhah, 23:3, 28). The festival days forbid melekhet 'avodah, "work of labor" (KJV "servile work"), that is, the regular work of one's trade. The rabbis concluded that cooking food is allowed on festivals but not on the Sabbath, as Exodus 12:16 already says: "what every person needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you" (Mishnah Megillah 1:5).

a: bring the priest a sheaf from the first of your harvest
p: The barley harvest began with a sheaf waved before God. Only then could the new crop be eaten.
b: Barley ripens in Israel in March and April, before wheat. The 'omer (a sheaf, also a dry measure) was the first cut, given to God before anyone ate bread, roasted grain or fresh ears from the new crop (23:14). Joshua 5:11 says Israel ate "roasted grain" from the land the day after Passover. The Mishnah describes messengers cutting the barley at dusk with crowds watching, and roasting and grinding it for the offering (Menachot 10:3–4). The gift says that the whole harvest is God's.

a: on the day after the Sabbath
p: Jews argued for centuries over this phrase. It decides the date of Shavuot (Pentecost).
b: If "the Sabbath" is the first day of Unleavened Bread, a rest day, the sheaf is waved on the 16th of the month and the Feast of Weeks always falls fifty days later. That was the Pharisees' view, kept by rabbinic Judaism; the Septuagint also reads "the day after the first day." The Boethusians and Sadducees (priestly parties of the Second Temple era), and later the Karaites (a Jewish movement that rejected rabbinic tradition), read "Sabbath" as the weekly Saturday, so the sheaf and Shavuot always fall on a Sunday (Mishnah Menachot 10:3; Talmud, Menachot 65a–66a). The book of Jubilees and the Dead Sea calendar put it on a Sunday after the festival week. Christians note that Jesus rose on "the first day of the week" and is called "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20).

a: seven Sabbaths. They must be full.
p: Jews still count the forty-nine days aloud, every evening, from Passover to Shavuot.
b: "Count for yourselves" became a nightly ritual, sefirat ha'omer: from the second night of Passover, observant Jews say a blessing and count the day, "Today is one day of the omer," up to forty-nine. The period became a time of semi-mourning in memory of Rabbi Akiva's students, who died in a plague according to the Talmud (Yevamot 62b), broken by the festive 33rd day, Lag Ba'omer. Kabbalists linked each day to a quality of the soul to be refined. "Sabbaths" here means full weeks, which is why the feast is called Weeks.

a: Count fifty days
p: In Greek "fiftieth" is pentēkostē, Pentecost. Acts 2 sets the coming of the Spirit on this day.
b: The feast later called Shavuot, "Weeks," was named Pentecost ("fiftieth") by Greek-speaking Jews (Tobit 2:1; 2 Maccabees 12:32). Exodus calls it the Feast of Harvest, "for the first crops of your work" (Exodus 23:16). The rabbis linked it to the giving of the Torah at Sinai, since Israel arrived there in the third month (Exodus 19:1; Talmud, Shabbat 86b), though Leviticus gives it only as a harvest feast. In Acts 2:1–41, the Spirit comes "when the day of Pentecost had come," with Jews from every nation in Jerusalem, and three thousand are baptized; many Christians see the harvest's first fruits and the new law written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
r: Exodus 23:16; Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 16:9–12; Acts 2:1–41; Acts 20:16; 1 Corinthians 16:8

a: baked with leaven
t: Leavened bread on the altar's feast
p: Leaven was banned from the altar, but these first-fruit loaves are leavened.
b: No grain offering burned on the altar could contain leaven (2:11). These two loaves are an exception: they are not burned but waved and given to the priest (23:20). Ordinary bread was leavened, so the people offer the bread they actually eat. Christian writers have read the two loaves in various ways, for example as Jews and Gentiles brought together at Pentecost; this is a later symbolic reading, not in the text.

a: Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner.
t: Gleaning in the middle of the calendar
p: The harvest-law of 19:9–10 is repeated in the middle of the feasts.
b: Why put a law about the poor in a festival calendar? Rashi answers: to teach that one who leaves gleanings for the poor is counted as if he had built the Temple and offered sacrifices in it. The harvest feast is where the poor share the harvest, as Deuteronomy 16:11 says of Weeks: rejoice "you, your son and daughter, your servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow." The book of Ruth, set between barley and wheat harvest (Ruth 1:22; 2:23), is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

a: a reminder made with loud blasts
t: The day of blasts: Rosh Hashanah
p: Leviticus does not call it a new year. Later Judaism made it Rosh Hashanah.
b: Zikhron teru'ah means a remembrance (or a reminder to God) by teru'ah, a loud blast or shout; Numbers 29:1 calls it "a day of blasting." The text does not say what instrument; Jewish tradition blows the ram's horn, the shofar, while the Septuagint says "trumpets." The Bible's year begins in spring (Exodus 12:2), but the Mishnah calls the first of the seventh month the new year for counting years (Rosh Hashanah 1:1), and it became the Day of Judgment opening ten Days of Awe before Yom Kippur. Some Christian interpreters, especially dispensationalists (who read prophecy as a timeline of future ages), link it to "the last trumpet" of Christ's return (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16); others see no such link in the text.
r: Numbers 10:10; Numbers 29:1–6; Nehemiah 8:2; Psalm 81:3; 1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16

a: You are to humble yourselves
p: The Hebrew is literally "afflict your souls." Jews have always understood it as fasting.
b: Ve'innitem et-nafshotekhem (KJV "afflict your souls") means to humble or deny oneself; Isaiah 58:3 and Psalm 35:13 pair it with fasting. The Mishnah lists five afflictions for Yom Kippur: no eating or drinking, washing, anointing with oil, wearing leather shoes, or marital relations (Yoma 8:1). Luke calls the day simply "the Fast" (Acts 27:9). Isaiah 58 warns that fasting without justice is not the fast God wants. The full Day of Atonement ritual is in chapter 16.

a: I will wipe out that person
p: Here God says not "he will be cut off" but "I will destroy him."
b: Leviticus usually says a sinner "will be cut off" (23:29); Peter joins that verse to Deuteronomy 18:19 in Acts 3:23. Here God says "I will destroy" (veha'avadti), the only time this verb is used of the penalty. Some rabbis read it as stronger, others as the same karet (see 17:4). The point is that no human court enforces the Day of Atonement; God sees whether a person keeps it.

a: from evening to evening
p: Jewish days run from evening to evening. This verse is a key source for that custom.
b: The Day of Atonement begins "on the ninth day of the month, in the evening" and runs to the next evening. Genesis 1 already counts "there was evening, and there was morning." Jewish holy days and the weekly Sabbath begin at sunset, which is why candles are lit on Friday evening. This verse led the rabbis to add time to the beginning and end of holy days, so that a little of the ninth becomes holy too (Talmud, Yoma 81b).

a: the Feast of Booths
p: The autumn harvest feast, also called Ingathering and Tabernacles. Israelites lived in branch huts for a week.
b: Exodus calls it "the Feast of Ingathering as the year goes out" (Exodus 23:16). Leviticus adds the booths (sukkot), temporary shelters of branches like those field workers built at harvest (Isaiah 1:8). It was the greatest feast of the year, simply "the feast" (1 Kings 8:2, 65); Solomon dedicated the Temple at it. The KJV's "tabernacles" comes from Latin tabernacula, "tents, huts," and has nothing to do with the tabernacle of Exodus, a different Hebrew word. Jews still build a sukkah and eat in it for seven days.
r: Exodus 23:16; Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; 1 Kings 8:2, 65; Nehemiah 8:14–18; Zechariah 14:16–19; John 7:2

a: It is the closing assembly.
p: 'Atseret means a holding back or closing assembly. Judaism keeps it as Shemini Atzeret.
b: 'Atseret comes from a verb meaning "to hold back, restrain": a solemn assembly that closes the festival, or a day of holding back from work. The rabbis pictured a king who asks his guests to stay one more day after a long feast (Rashi). Shemini Atzeret, "the eighth day of assembly," is a festival of its own, and in later times the yearly cycle of Torah reading came to end and restart on it or the next day, Simchat Torah, "joy of the Torah." John 7:37 may refer to this day: "The festival came to its last and great day. Jesus stood there and cried out..."

a: when you have gathered in what the land produces
p: Critics see harvest festivals that were later tied to the exodus. Traditional readers see both from the start.
b: Leviticus dates the feasts by the calendar but also ties them to the farm year: barley (the sheaf), wheat (Weeks), and the fall harvest of grapes and olives (Booths). Only Booths is linked to the exodus, in 23:43. Julius Wellhausen argued that Israel's feasts began as Canaanite farm festivals and were later "historicized" with stories of the exodus; the Priestly writers then fixed them to exact dates. Traditional scholars reply that the Bible ties the feasts to history from the beginning (Exodus 12; 23:15) and that remembering God's acts in the yearly round is the point. Many moderns hold a middle view.

a: the fruit of beautiful trees, palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees and poplars of the valley stream
p: Jewish tradition reads these as the etrog, the lulav, myrtle and willow, waved together at Sukkot.
b: The rabbis identified "the fruit of beautiful trees" (peri 'ets hadar) as the citron (etrog), "thick-leaved trees" as myrtle, and the "poplars" ('arvei nachal) as willow branches; with the palm branch (lulav) these are the four species waved in all directions at Sukkot (Mishnah Sukkah 3). Josephus tells how worshipers pelted King Alexander Jannaeus with citrons at the altar (Antiquities 13.372). In Nehemiah 8:15 the branches are used to build the booths instead. Midrash compares the four to four kinds of Jews, with and without learning and good deeds, all bound together (Leviticus Rabbah 30:12). Crowds waved palm branches when Jesus entered Jerusalem (John 12:13).

a: Rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days
p: Booths is the feast of joy. The water-drawing celebration of Jesus' day was its high point.
b: Deuteronomy 16:14–15 says, "you will be nothing but glad." In Second Temple times, priests poured water at the altar each morning of Sukkot, and the nights blazed with torches and dancing: "whoever has not seen the joy of the water-drawing has never seen joy in his life" (Mishnah Sukkah 5:1). John sets Jesus' cry, "If someone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink... rivers of living water," and his words "I am the light of the world" at this feast (John 7:37–38; 8:12). Zechariah pictures all nations coming up yearly to keep Sukkot (Zechariah 14:16).

a: I made the Israelites live in booths
p: Did Israel live in huts in the wilderness, or under God's cloud? The rabbis disagreed.
b: Exodus speaks of tents, not huts, in the wilderness. Rabbi Akiva said the booths were real huts; Rabbi Eliezer said they were the clouds of glory that sheltered Israel (Talmud, Sukkah 11b). Either way the feast makes each generation relive the journey, sitting in a fragile shelter under the sky. Nehemiah 8:17 says Israel had not lived in booths "since the days of Jeshua son of Nun" until after the exile, which critics read as evidence the custom was new, and others as a statement about the joy or scale of that celebration. John 1:14 says the Word "pitched his tent" (eskēnōsen) among us, a word Christians often connect with this feast.

a: So Moses told the Israelites the LORD's set times.
p: Many Christians read the seven festivals as a map of salvation. Others think this goes beyond the text.
b: A widely taught Christian reading sets the feasts in order as stages of God's plan: Passover, the cross; Unleavened Bread, Christ's sinless body; First Fruits, the resurrection; Weeks, the Spirit at Pentecost; Blasts, the return of Christ; Atonement, Israel's repentance (Zechariah 12:10) or Christ's work (Hebrews 9); Booths, God dwelling with his people (Revelation 21:3). The New Testament makes some of these links itself (1 Corinthians 5:7; 15:20; Acts 2), but the later ones are inferences. Colossians 2:16–17 calls festivals "a shadow of the things to come." Jews keep them as living commands, and some Christian and Messianic Jewish groups keep them too.
r: 1 Corinthians 5:7–8; 1 Corinthians 15:20; Acts 2:1; Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 9:11–12; Zechariah 14:16; Revelation 21:3

a: so that a lamp can be lit to burn always
t: The lamp that never goes out
p: These verses repeat Exodus 27:20–21 almost word for word.
b: Exodus already commanded, "bring you pure oil pressed from olives for the light, so that a lamp can be lit to burn always" (Exodus 27:20). Leviticus repeats it here in the same words, perhaps because the oil and bread are continual offerings that frame the feasts, daily and weekly beside the yearly calendar. "Always" (tamid) means regularly, every evening to morning (24:3), not literally nonstop. Synagogues keep a ner tamid, an "eternal light," above the ark. The story of Hanukkah, when a small jar of oil lasted eight days, is told in the Talmud (Shabbat 21b), not in the books of Maccabees.

a: bake it into twelve ring-shaped loaves
p: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set before God every Sabbath. David and Jesus both appear in its story.
b: Exodus calls it "the Presence Bread" (Exodus 25:30), bread set before God's face. The twelve challot (perhaps ring-shaped or pierced loaves, the word behind today's Sabbath challah) stand for the tribes. Each loaf used two tenths of an ephah, a large loaf. When David was fleeing Saul, the priest at Nob gave him this holy bread (1 Samuel 21:1–6), and Jesus cited the story when his disciples picked grain on a Sabbath (Mark 2:25–26). The Talmud tells that the bread stayed fresh and warm all week (Chagigah 26b).

a: as its token portion
p: The frankincense is burned as a "memorial," the part that reminds God.
b: Azkarah comes from zakhar, "remember." It is the part of a grain offering burned on the altar (2:2, 9, 16); here the frankincense is burned in place of the bread, which the priests eat. The idea is that the offering "reminds" God of the worshiper. Acts 10:4 uses the same picture: Cornelius's prayers and gifts "have gone up as a memorial before God."

a: the son of an Israelite woman, whose father was an Egyptian
p: The man's mixed parentage is stressed. The rabbis built a backstory; moderns ask why the detail is there.
b: He is one of the "mixed crowd" that left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38). The rabbis said his father was the Egyptian taskmaster whom Moses killed (Exodus 2:11–12), and that the fight was over where he could camp, since tribes camped by their fathers' lines (Sifra; Rashi). Modern scholars note that the case raises a legal question: does the law of blasphemy apply to one who is half outsider? The answer comes in 24:16 and 24:22: one law for the foreigner and the native-born.

a: spoke the Name with contempt and cursed
p: The verb can mean "pierce" or "designate." The rabbis read it as pronouncing the divine name.
b: Vayyiqqov comes from naqav, which means "to pierce" (2 Kings 12:9) and also "to designate, name" (Numbers 1:17; Isaiah 62:2). So the man may have "cursed by naming the Name" or "insulted the Name." "The Name" (hashem) stands for YHWH. The rabbis held that blasphemy required pronouncing the divine name itself (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). Here is one root of the Jewish custom of not saying YHWH aloud, reading "Adonai" or "Hashem" instead, which English Bibles follow by printing "the LORD." See also 24:16.

a: Shelomith daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan
p: Only the mother is named. The rabbis read meaning into her name; some moderns see a slur on Dan.
b: The Bible rarely names minor characters, yet here we learn the mother's name, father and tribe, while the man is nameless. Rashi, following the midrash, played on her names: Shelomith always said "shalom" to everyone, and Dibri "chattered" (dibber) with everyone, as if her friendliness had led her to an Egyptian. Some modern scholars think naming Dan, a tribe later remembered for idolatry (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29), is a quiet comment. Others see simple record keeping. The text itself passes no judgment on her.

a: so that the LORD's own word would make the case clear to them
p: One of four cases in the Torah where Moses has to ask God what to do.
b: Moses does not know the penalty, so the man is held "at the mouth of the LORD." The same happens with men unclean at Passover (Numbers 9:6–14), the Sabbath wood-gatherer (Numbers 15:32–36), and Zelophehad's daughters (Numbers 27:1–11). These stories show law growing case by case, and the rabbis noted that even Moses had to ask. The answer here becomes a general law (24:15–22), a pattern ancient law collections also used.

a: All who heard him are to lean their hands on his head
p: The witnesses lay hands on him before the stoning. Why?
b: Leaning hands on a sacrifice identifies it with the worshiper (1:4), and on the Day of Atonement the high priest lays hands on the goat to transfer Israel's sins (16:21). Here the hearers lay hands on the man. Some read it as returning to him the guilt they took on by hearing the curse (Milgrom); others as formal testimony, "his blood is on his own head" (Sifra); others as a public act that makes the community responsible for the sentence. Susanna 1:34 shows the same gesture at a trial.

a: Whoever speaks the name of the LORD with contempt must be put to death.
t: Blasphemy, from Sinai to the Sanhedrin
p: This law shaped how Jews treat God's name, and it stands behind charges against Jesus and Stephen.
b: The Septuagint reads, "whoever names the name of the Lord," and Philo took it to mean that even uttering the Name carelessly deserved death (Life of Moses 2.203–206). Rabbinic law required the actual Name to be spoken, and the witnesses repeated the words in private at the trial, with the judges tearing their clothes (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). Jesus was accused of blasphemy (Mark 14:64; John 10:33), and Stephen was stoned for it (Acts 6:11; 7:58). Christian states long punished blasphemy, citing this verse; most modern democracies have repealed such laws, though some countries still enforce them.

a: life for life
p: The same "life for life" formula as Exodus 21:23, here for an animal: make it good.
b: For a killed animal, "life for life" plainly means compensation: give an animal of equal value. The rabbis argued that the same logic holds for injuries to people (24:19–20): "eye for eye" means payment of the eye's value, since one eye is not the same as another (Talmud, Bava Kamma 83b–84a). Exodus says, "you are to give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (Exodus 21:23–24). The verb "make it good" (shillem) is related to shalom, wholeness.

a: If anyone puts a defect on his fellow citizen
t: The same word as the priest's defect
p: Mum, a "defect," is the word used of blemished priests and animals in chapters 21–22.
b: The Hebrew says literally "gives a defect" (mum) to his neighbor. It is the word that disqualified priests (21:17–23) and animals (22:20–25). The Plain text keeps "defect" so readers can see the link: to maim a person is to damage someone made in God's image (Genesis 9:6). The rule of equal payback, called lex talionis or the talion principle, "as he has done, so it will be done to him," limits revenge to the measure of the harm.

a: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
p: Jesus quotes this law in the Sermon on the Mount. Readers debate what he rejected.
b: "You have heard what was said: 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.' But I myself tell you: do not set yourself against the evil person" (Matthew 5:38–39). Jewish scholars point out that by Jesus' time the law was already applied as money damages, and that it was meant for courts, to keep punishment proportionate, not for private revenge. Many Christians read Jesus as speaking about personal response, not courts; others (Tolstoy, many Anabaptists) read him as rejecting retaliation altogether. Exodus 21:24–25 lists more pairs: "hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn."

a: You are to have one law for foreigner and native-born alike
p: The case of the half-Egyptian ends with equality before the law.
b: The story began with a man of mixed parentage; it ends with the principle: mishpat echad, one judgment, for the foreigner as for the native-born. Exodus 12:49 says the same of the Passover: "One teaching will hold for the one born in the land and for the foreigner who lives among you" (Exodus 12:49; compare Numbers 15:15–16). The foreigner is protected by the law and also bound by it. Many see here an early form of equal treatment under law.

a: on Mount Sinai
p: Chapters 25–27 are set at Sinai itself, though the rest of Leviticus is spoken from the tent.
b: Leviticus opens with God speaking "from the tent of meeting" (1:1), yet here and in 26:46 and 27:34 the setting is "Mount Sinai." The rabbis famously asked, "What does the Sabbath year have to do with Mount Sinai?" and answered: just as the Sabbath year was given in full detail at Sinai, so were all the commandments (Sifra; Rashi). Critical scholars see the phrase as a frame that ties the Holiness Code to the Sinai covenant, closing the section that began in Exodus 19. The weekly reading 25:1–26:2 is called Behar, "on the mountain."

a: the land is to rest, a Sabbath for the LORD
p: Every seventh year the land lay fallow. History shows Jews keeping it at least in the Second Temple era.
b: Exodus already commanded it: "in the seventh year let it go and leave it alone, so that the needy of your people can eat from it" (Exodus 23:11), and Deuteronomy 15:1–11 adds a release of debts. The returning exiles pledged to keep it (Nehemiah 10:31). 1 Maccabees 6:49, 53 reports a siege lost for lack of food "because it was a sabbath year for the land." Josephus says Julius Caesar excused the Jews from tax in the seventh year (Antiquities 14.202), and Tacitus sneered that Jews gave every seventh year to idleness (Histories 5.4). Jewish farmers in Israel still observe shemittah, often by a legal sale of the land to a non-Jew for the year, a practice debated since 1889.

a: your untrimmed vines
p: The word for an unpruned vine is nazir, the same as the Nazirite who leaves his hair uncut.
b: 'Inevei nezirekha, "grapes of your nazir," calls the unpruned vine a Nazirite: like the man under a Nazirite vow, it grows untouched, its "hair" uncut (Numbers 6:5). The image makes the land itself holy in its rest year, dedicated to God. The KJV's "vine undressed" gives the sense.

a: What the land gives in its Sabbath will be food for all of you
p: The rest year feeds owners, slaves, workers, lodgers and animals alike.
b: In the Sabbath year no one owns the crop. What grows by itself is food for the owner and the slave, the hired worker, the lodger and the wild animals together. Exodus stresses the poor (Exodus 23:11); Leviticus stresses equality: for one year everyone eats from the same field. Ecologists and some Christian and Jewish environmental writers point to the land's rest as a model of caring for the earth; others caution that the text's purpose is religious, the land as God's.

a: the ram's horn
p: The Jubilee opened with the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement.
b: The shofar is a ram's horn, the instrument of Sinai (Exodus 19:16, 19), war (Joshua 6) and coronation (1 Kings 1:34). Opening the Jubilee on the Day of Atonement joins forgiveness and release: when Israel is made right with God, debts and slavery are undone. The word "jubilee" comes through Latin iubilaeus from Hebrew yovel, which means a ram or ram's horn (Joshua 6:4–5); the Latin was influenced by iubilare, "to shout for joy."

a: proclaim release in the land for all who live in it
t: Deror: liberty, and the Liberty Bell
p: The KJV's "proclaim liberty throughout all the land" is cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.
b: Deror means release, freedom from debt or bondage, the cognate of Akkadian andurāru, the release that Babylonian kings sometimes decreed when they canceled debts on taking the throne (Moshe Weinfeld). Jeremiah 34:8–17 uses it of Zedekiah's slave release, and Isaiah 61:1 of "release to the captives." The bell ordered for the Pennsylvania State House in 1751 carries the KJV words, "Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof. Lev. XXV. v X." In the 1830s abolitionists named it the Liberty Bell and made it a symbol of freeing the slaves.

a: It will be a Jubilee for you.
p: No biblical story shows a Jubilee being kept. Scholars split between an ideal and a real but forgotten law.
b: The Bible never records a Jubilee. The rabbis said it was kept only while all the tribes lived in the land and ceased when Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh were exiled (Sifra; Talmud, Arakhin 32b). Julius Wellhausen and many critical scholars call it a utopian program, written late. Others think it reforms an older practice of royal releases known across the ancient Near East (Weinfeld), or was observed in early times and lapsed (Robert North). John Bergsma traces how later writers, from Isaiah 61 and Daniel 9 to the book of Jubilees and the Dead Sea Scrolls, turned it into a hope for a final age of release. Second Chronicles 36:21 counts the exile as the land's long-missed Sabbaths (see 26:34).

a: each of you is to go back to his own holding
p: Jesus' first sermon in Luke reads Isaiah 61, the Jubilee prophecy, and says it is fulfilled.
b: Isaiah 61:1–2 uses Jubilee language: "to proclaim release to the captives... to proclaim a year of the LORD's goodwill." A Dead Sea scroll, 11QMelchizedek, combines this very verse (25:13) with Isaiah 61 and pictures Melchizedek proclaiming a final release in the tenth jubilee. In Luke 4:16–21 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue and says, "Today this writing has been fulfilled in your ears." Sharon Ringe and John Howard Yoder argued that Jesus announced a real Jubilee of social release; others read his words as spiritual release from sin, using the Greek aphesis, "release, forgiveness," for both.

a: do not wrong one another
p: From this verse came Jewish law against price gouging, and against hurtful words.
b: The verb honah means to wrong or oppress. The rabbis made this verse the source of ona'at mammon, overcharging: a sale more than one sixth above or below fair price could be undone (Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3). From 25:17, the repeated command, they derived ona'at devarim, wronging with words: reminding a convert of his past, or asking a seller the price with no intent to buy (Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10). The Talmud says that shaming someone in public is like shedding blood (Bava Metzia 58b).

a: what he is selling you is a number of crops
p: Land sales were really leases until the Jubilee. The price depends on the years left.
b: Because land returns to its family at the Jubilee, a "sale" buys only the crops until then. With forty years left, the price is high; with two, it is low. Jeremiah's purchase of his cousin's field, with deeds sealed in a jar, shows family land and the right of redemption at work (Jeremiah 32:6–15). Ahab's desire for Naboth's vineyard runs into the same idea: "The LORD keep me from giving you my fathers' inheritance!" (1 Kings 21:3).

a: I will order my blessing for you in the sixth year
p: The Sabbath year asks for trust. God promises the sixth year will carry them.
b: The question "What will we eat?" is real: a year without planting means hunger in the eighth year too, until the new crop. God's answer echoes the manna: on the sixth day there was a double portion so the people could rest (Exodus 16:22–29). Jesus uses the same logic: "Stop asking, 'What are we going to eat?'... Seek God's kingdom and his righteousness before anything else" (Matthew 6:31–33).

a: the land is mine. You are foreigners and lodgers living with me.
p: Israel holds the land as God's tenants. The verse has fed debates on property and justice.
b: "To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it" (Psalm 24:1). Israel lives on God's land as gerim vetoshavim, foreigners and lodgers, the same status the poor foreigner has among Israelites. Abraham told the Hittites, "I am a foreigner living among you as a settler" (Genesis 23:4), and David prays, "we are foreigners before you, and lodgers, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15). Hebrews and 1 Peter call believers "strangers and temporary residents on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11). The idea that no family may lose its land for good has inspired land reformers, debt-relief campaigns and liberation theologians; others caution against reading a modern economic program into a tribal land law.
r: Genesis 23:4; 1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 24:1; Psalm 39:12; Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11

a: his closest family redeemer
p: The family redeemer buys back land or relatives. Ruth's Boaz is the famous example.
b: The go'el is the nearest male relative who steps in to rescue: he buys back family land (25:25), redeems a relative sold into slavery (25:48–49), and avenges a murdered kinsman (Numbers 35:19). In Ruth 4, Boaz redeems the field of Elimelech and marries Ruth. The prophets call God himself Israel's go'el (Isaiah 41:14; 43:14), and Job cries, "I know that my redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). Christians apply the title to Christ, whose "redemption" buys people back (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 1:18–19).
r: 25:48–49; Numbers 35:19; Ruth 3:9–13; Ruth 4:1–10; Jeremiah 32:7; Isaiah 43:14; Job 19:25

a: a walled city
p: City houses could be sold for good after a year. Village houses belonged with the farmland.
b: The Jubilee protects the family farm, the base of Israel's tribal life. A house in a walled city was not tied to fields, so it could be sold permanently, with only a year to redeem it. Village houses counted as part of the farmland and returned at the Jubilee. Scholars see here a law shaped for an agricultural society with growing towns, and some date the law by this mix of town and country, though the setting fits many periods.

a: the cities of the Levites
p: The Levites had no tribal land, only towns and pastures. Their houses could always be redeemed.
b: Numbers 35:1–8 and Joshua 21 assign forty-eight towns, with surrounding pasture, to the Levites, who had no tribal territory. Since a house was all a Levite family owned, its houses are treated like farmland: always redeemable and returned at the Jubilee. The pastures could never be sold (25:34). Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, sold a field and gave the money to the apostles (Acts 4:36–37), which shows that by then Levites did own land.

a: hold him up. Like a foreigner or a lodger he is to live on with you.
p: The Hebrew is compressed. Does "foreigner or lodger" describe the poor brother, or extend help to outsiders?
b: Literally: "you shall hold him up, a foreigner and lodger, and he shall live with you." Most read it as "support him as you would a resident foreigner": he lives with you as a dependent, but must not be exploited. The KJV reads it as "though he be a stranger," so the duty reaches outsiders too. The rabbis read "hold him up" as help before he falls: "like a load on a donkey; while it is still on the donkey, one person can hold it; once it falls, five cannot lift it" (Sifra). Maimonides ranked the highest form of charity as helping someone become self-supporting, with a gift, loan or partnership.
orig: וְהֶחֱזַקְתָּ בּוֹ גֵּר וְתוֹשָׁב (vehecheziqta bo ger vetoshav)

a: Do not take interest or profit from him.
p: The ban on interest shaped Jewish, Christian and Islamic economics for two thousand years.
b: Neshekh means "bite," interest taken up front; tarbit is "increase," interest added later. Exodus forbids interest to the poor (Exodus 22:25), and Deuteronomy allows it from a foreigner but not a brother (Deuteronomy 23:19–20). Medieval church councils forbade Christians to lend at interest at all, which pushed many Jews into moneylending, with tragic results. John Calvin, in a letter of 1545, argued that the law targeted exploiting the poor, not all interest, and modern banking grew from that view. Jewish law permits business investment through a partnership contract (heter iska). Islamic finance still forbids interest (riba).
r: Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Psalm 15:5; Ezekiel 18:8, 13, 17; Nehemiah 5:1–13; Luke 6:34–35

a: do not make him work the work of a slave
p: Exodus and Deuteronomy free a Hebrew slave after six years; Leviticus says at the Jubilee. How do they fit?
b: Exodus says, "If you acquire a Hebrew slave, he is to work six years. In the seventh he goes free" (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12). Leviticus says an Israelite who sells himself is not a slave at all but like a hired worker, freed at the Jubilee. The rabbis harmonized: six years for one sold by a court for theft, the Jubilee for one who sold himself, and the Jubilee frees even a slave who chose to stay for life (Talmud, Kiddushin 14b–15a). Critical scholars see laws from different times; Jeremiah 34 shows the six-year law being broken. Leviticus's claim is radical: an Israelite cannot really be owned, because he belongs to God (25:42).

a: For they are my servants
p: The same word, eved, means servant and slave. Israel cannot be enslaved because it already belongs to God.
b: God brought Israel out of the house of slaves to be his 'avadim, servants (25:55). The Plain text uses "servants" for God's people and "slaves" for human ownership, but the Hebrew word is the same. The argument is that no Israelite can be sold "the way a slave is sold," because God's servants are not for sale. Paul uses the same logic: "You were bought for a price. Do not become slaves of other people" (1 Corinthians 7:23), and calls himself "a slave of Christ Jesus" (Romans 1:1).

a: with crushing cruelty
p: The word perekh is used of Egypt's treatment of Israel. Do not do to others what Egypt did to you.
b: Befarekh, "with harshness," appears in the Torah only here (25:43, 46, 53) and in Exodus 1:13–14: "The Egyptians made the Israelites serve them with crushing cruelty." The Plain text uses the same words in both books so readers can hear the echo. Israel must not become Egypt. Ezekiel accuses Israel's shepherds of ruling "with force and with crushing cruelty" (Ezekiel 34:4).

a: from them you may buy slaves, men and women
p: Leviticus allows Israelites to own foreigners as slaves for life. Americans fought over this verse.
b: The release laws protect Israelites only. Foreigners, and the children of resident foreigners, could be bought and passed on as property "for good" (25:46). Other laws still limited cruelty to such slaves (Exodus 21:20–21, 26–27; Deuteronomy 23:15–16). In the American slavery debate, defenders such as Thornton Stringfellow cited this passage as proof that God allowed slavery; abolitionists answered with the Jubilee's "proclaim liberty" (25:10, KJV), the kidnapping law (Exodus 21:16), and the dignity of every person in God's image (Genesis 1:27). Mark Noll calls this a crisis of how to read the Bible. Most Jews and Christians today read the law as a concession to an ancient economy, not a pattern to follow.

a: If a foreigner or lodger among you prospers
p: An Israelite sold to a foreigner must be redeemed by family. The rabbis made ransoming captives a great duty.
b: The law assumes foreigners could become rich and own Israelites, and insists on their redemption by brothers, uncles or cousins. Jewish communities in the Middle Ages made pidyon shevuyim, ransoming captives, one of their highest charities; Maimonides called it greater than feeding the poor. Nehemiah reminds the rich that the community had bought back Jews sold to foreigners, only for them to sell their brothers again (Nehemiah 5:8).

a: a standing stone
p: Matzevot, standing stones, were once set up by Jacob, but later were banned.
b: A matzevah is an upright stone. Jacob set one up at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), and Moses set up twelve at Sinai (Exodus 24:4); archaeologists have found such stones in Israelite shrines, as at Arad. Later laws ban them as part of Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 16:22). The "stone carved with figures" (even maskit) was probably a stone with carved images, of the kind Ezekiel saw on the Temple walls (Ezekiel 8:10–12). Verses 1–2 sum up the covenant's demands before the blessings and curses: no idols, keep the Sabbaths, fear the sanctuary.

a: If you walk in my rules
p: Ancient treaties ended with blessings and curses. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 follow the pattern.
b: Treaties between great kings and their vassals, from the Hittites to the Assyrians, closed with blessings for loyalty and long lists of curses for rebellion. The Vassal Treaties of Esarhaddon (672 BC) curse rebels with ground like iron and a sky like bronze that gives no rain, closely parallel to 26:19 and Deuteronomy 28:23. Scholars debate whether Israel borrowed from Assyrian models (seventh century) or from older Hittite ones (second millennium); traditional scholars favor the earlier. Either way, the covenant at Sinai is shaped like a treaty, with God as king. Leviticus has a short list of blessings and a much longer list of curses, as Deuteronomy does.

a: I will give you your rains at their proper time
p: Israel's farms lived on rain, not rivers. The early and late rains made or broke a year.
b: Unlike Egypt, watered by the Nile, Canaan depends on rain "from the sky" (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). The early rains in October and November soften the ground for plowing; the late rains in March and April fill the grain. When they come "at their proper time," the harvest runs from barley to wheat to grapes to sowing with no gap (26:5). Baal was Canaan's storm god, so promising rain is also a claim that the LORD, not Baal, sends it (1 Kings 17–18; Hosea 2:8).
r: Deuteronomy 11:10–17; Deuteronomy 28:12; 1 Kings 17:1; Joel 2:23; Hosea 2:8; James 5:7

a: I will give peace in the land
p: Peace, safety and no wild beasts: the picture returns in the prophets' visions of the end.
b: Shalom here is security: lying down unafraid, no dangerous animals, no invading army. Ezekiel's "covenant of peace" repeats these words, removing wild beasts and letting people sleep in the woods (Ezekiel 34:25–28), and Micah pictures each one under his vine and fig tree "and no one will make them afraid" (Micah 4:4). Isaiah goes further, with wolf and lamb together (Isaiah 11:6–9).

a: I will make you bear fruit and grow many
p: The first blessing, "Be fruitful and grow many," returns as a covenant promise.
b: The words echo God's first blessing on humanity, "Be fruitful and grow many" (Genesis 1:28), and his promises to Abraham and Jacob (Genesis 17:6; 35:11). Exodus begins with Israel in Egypt growing exactly this way (Exodus 1:7). The covenant at Sinai keeps the promise to the fathers alive, and 26:42 will name Jacob, Isaac and Abraham.

a: I will set my dwelling among you
p: The highest blessing is God's presence. Paul and Revelation both quote these verses.
b: Mishkani, "my dwelling," is the word for the tabernacle (Exodus 25:9). The blessings climb from rain to peace to this: God himself living among them. Ezekiel 37:27 repeats it: "My dwelling place will be with them. I will be their God, and they will be my people." Paul combines 26:11–12 with Ezekiel to call the church "the temple of the living God" (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation 21:3 hears it at the end: "Look! God's tent is with human beings" (the Greek word for "tent" is skēnē). The Septuagint here reads "my covenant" instead of "my dwelling" (see variants).
r: Exodus 25:8–9; Exodus 29:45–46; Ezekiel 37:26–27; 2 Corinthians 6:16; John 1:14; Revelation 21:3

a: I will walk about among you
p: The verb is the one used of God walking in the garden. The covenant restores Eden's closeness.
b: Vehithallakhti, "I will walk about," is the same form used when Adam and Eve "heard the sound of the LORD God walking about in the garden in the breezy part of the day" (Genesis 3:8). Many readers see the tabernacle as a new Eden, with its cherubim, lampstand like a tree, and gold (Wenham). The covenant formula that follows, "I will be your God, and you will be my people," runs through the whole Bible (Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).
r: Genesis 3:8; Deuteronomy 23:14; 2 Samuel 7:6–7; Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 6:16

a: made you walk upright
p: God broke the yoke and let Israel stand tall. The rabbis heard a promise of height and dignity.
b: A yoke bar pressed the necks of oxen or slaves down; God broke its bars (Jeremiah 28:2, 10–13; Ezekiel 34:27). Qomemiyyut, "upright," appears only here. Jewish prayer asks God to "lead us upright (qomemiyyut) to our land," in the blessing before the Shema. Jesus offers a yoke that is "easy" (Matthew 11:29–30), and Paul tells the Galatians not to take up again "a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1).
r: Jeremiah 28:10–13; Ezekiel 34:27; Isaiah 9:4; Matthew 11:29–30; Galatians 5:1; Luke 13:11–13

a: I will bring on you sudden terror, wasting disease and fever
p: Jews call this passage the Tokhechah, "the rebuke." In synagogue it is read quickly and in a low voice.
b: The curses of 26:14–43 and Deuteronomy 28:15–68 are called tokhechah, "rebuke." The Talmud says they must not be broken up but read as one section by one reader, "so that the curses not be cut short" (Megillah 31b), and many congregations read them in an undertone. Some Jews avoid being called up for that reading, and in some communities the reader takes it himself. The rabbis also noted that the Leviticus curses are spoken by God in the first person ("I will") and are followed by a promise of return (26:40–45).

a: seven times over for your sins
p: The refrain "seven times" structures the curses into rising stages.
b: Four times God says he will punish "seven times" for their sins (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Seven is a number of fullness. The curses come in waves, each starting "if... you will not listen," each worse than the last: disease and defeat, drought, wild beasts, war and siege, and finally exile. The pattern shows that each blow is meant to turn the people back before the next: "If even after these things you will not let me correct you" (26:23). Amos 4:6–11 lists disasters in the same spirit, ending each with "yet you did not return to me."

a: I will make your sky like iron and your ground like bronze
p: Deuteronomy reverses the metals. An Assyrian treaty uses the same curse.
b: Deuteronomy says "The sky above you will turn to bronze, and the ground below you to iron" (Deuteronomy 28:23). Either way the sky gives no rain and the ground yields nothing. Esarhaddon's treaty curses rebels: "may they make your ground like iron... as rain does not fall from a bronze sky" (Vassal Treaties §63–64). The similarity is one reason scholars compare Israel's covenant with Assyrian treaties.

a: If you go on walking against me
p: Qeri appears only in this chapter. It may mean hostility, or acting as if things happen by chance.
b: Qeri (26:21, 23, 24, 27, 28, 40, 41) comes from a root meaning "to meet" or "to happen." Most translations take it as opposition: "walk contrary to me" (KJV), "in hostility." Maimonides read it as "by chance": if you treat disasters as accidents rather than as God's call to return, God will also treat you "by chance," leaving you to the world's fury (Mishneh Torah, Fasts 1:3). The Plain text gives the common sense, "walking against." The same word describes both Israel's conduct and God's response (26:24, 28): punishment fits the sin.

a: a sword on you that takes the revenge of the covenant
p: God's punishment is enforcement of a broken covenant, not random anger.
b: Neqam berit: the sword avenges the covenant itself. In ancient treaties, the gods were witnesses who punished breach; here God is both party and judge. "Staff of bread" (26:26) pictures bread as what a person leans on; Ezekiel uses the phrase for the siege of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4:16; 5:16; 14:13). The language of 26:25–26, sword, plague and famine, is the triad Jeremiah and Ezekiel repeat again and again for the fall of Jerusalem.
r: 26:26; Ezekiel 4:16; Ezekiel 5:16–17; Ezekiel 14:13; Jeremiah 14:12; Jeremiah 24:10; Haggai 1:6; Micah 6:14

a: You will eat the flesh of your sons
p: This curse came true in sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem, as the Bible and Josephus record.
b: During the Aramean siege of Samaria two mothers agreed to eat their sons (2 Kings 6:26–29). Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon: "Women known for compassion boiled their own children with their own hands" (Lamentations 4:10; 2:20). Josephus tells of a woman named Mary who ate her child during the Roman siege of AD 70 (Jewish War 6.201–213). The curse is not God's wish but a picture of what war and siege do to people when the covenant's protection is gone.
r: Deuteronomy 28:53–57; 2 Kings 6:26–29; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; Ezekiel 5:10; Jeremiah 19:9

a: I will throw your corpses on the corpses of your idols
p: The word for idols, gillulim, may be a slur meaning "dung balls." Ezekiel uses it 39 times.
b: Gillulim is probably related to galal, "dung," and sounds like a mocking name for idols, "dung-gods" or "lumps." It appears here and especially in Ezekiel, another link between the two. "Corpses of your idols" is bitter irony: the idols are as dead as the worshipers lying on them. "High places" (bamot) were hilltop shrines, and "incense stands" (chammanim) were small altars, some of which have been found in excavations.

a: And you I will scatter among the nations
p: The chapter ends in exile. Was it written before or after Israel's exile?
b: Assyria scattered the northern kingdom in 722 BC and Babylon took Judah in 586 BC. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take Leviticus 26 as Moses' prophecy, fulfilled centuries later. Many critical scholars think the exile passages (26:33–45) were written or expanded during or after the Babylonian exile, which they describe so closely; Jacob Milgrom held that most of the chapter is older, from the eighth century, when Assyria's deportations were already known, with a few exilic additions. The chapter's influence on Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Daniel is clear either way. Jews read the long dispersion after AD 70 through it too, as do Christian writers on Israel's history.

a: Then the land will make up for its Sabbaths
p: Chronicles reads the Babylonian exile as the land catching up on missed Sabbath years.
b: The verb ratsah means to pay off or to be satisfied: the land "pays itself" the rest years it was denied. Second Chronicles 36:21 joins this verse to Jeremiah's seventy years: "until the land had made up its Sabbaths... to fulfill seventy years." Seventy Sabbath years would be 490 years of neglect, which Daniel 9:24 turns into "seventy weeks" of years before a final atonement. The same verb returns in 26:41 and 26:43: the people "make up for" their guilt, as the land makes up for its Sabbaths.

a: The sound of a leaf blown about will chase them
p: Fear itself becomes the enemy. Proverbs and Isaiah use the same picture.
b: The exiles will flee from the rustle of a driven leaf, "with no one chasing," reversing the blessing in which five chase a hundred (26:8). Proverbs 28:1 says, "The wicked flee with no one after them." Isaiah 30:17 warns that a thousand will flee at the threat of one.

a: because of their fathers' guilt as well
p: Do children suffer for their parents' sins? Leviticus, Jeremiah and Ezekiel answer differently.
b: Exodus 20:5 speaks of guilt visited on the third and fourth generation of those who hate God. Here the exiles rot away in their own guilt and their fathers' too. Jeremiah and Ezekiel reject the proverb "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb" (Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–4): each dies for his own sin. Many readers reconcile them: children suffer the consequences of their parents' sins when they continue in them, which is why the next verse calls them to confess both (26:40). Daniel and Nehemiah do exactly that (Daniel 9:16; Nehemiah 9:2).
r: 26:40; Exodus 20:5–6; Exodus 34:7; Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–20; Daniel 9:16; Nehemiah 9:2

a: Then they will confess their guilt and their fathers' guilt
p: The Hebrew can be read as "they will confess" or "if they confess." Translations divide.
b: The verb vehitvaddu is a simple "and they will confess." Many versions, including the KJV and BSB, read it as a condition, "if they confess," linked to the "if" in 26:41. Others, including the Plain text, read a promise: in exile they will confess. The difference matters for theology: is restoration earned by repentance, or does God bring about the repentance he requires (Deuteronomy 30:6)? Daniel 9:4–19, Nehemiah 9 and Ezra 9 are confessions that follow this verse closely, and the Jewish confession of Yom Kippur, "we have sinned, we and our fathers," echoes it.

a: their uncircumcised heart
p: A heart that is closed to God. The prophets and Paul make this image central.
b: An "uncircumcised" organ is blocked: uncircumcised lips cannot speak (Exodus 6:12), ears cannot hear (Jeremiah 6:10), a heart cannot respond. Deuteronomy calls Israel to "circumcise your hearts" (Deuteronomy 10:16) and promises that God will do it (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah warns that Israel is uncircumcised in heart like the nations (Jeremiah 9:25–26). Stephen accuses his judges of being "uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears" (Acts 7:51), and Paul writes that true circumcision is "of the heart, in spirit and not in letter" (Romans 2:29).
r: 19:23; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:25–26; Acts 7:51; Romans 2:28–29

a: then I will remember my covenant with Jacob
p: Only here are the patriarchs named from last to first.
b: Everywhere else the order is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Here it runs backward. Rashi suggests that if Jacob's merit is not enough, Isaac's will be added, and if not, Abraham's. Others think memory is pictured reaching back in time, generation by generation, to the first promise. Also unusual: God promises to remember "the land" as though it were a covenant partner, as in 25:23. "Remember" in the Bible means to act on a promise, as in Egypt: "God remembered his covenant, the one with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob" (Exodus 2:24).

a: I will not reject them
p: Even in exile God will not break his covenant with Israel. Jews and Christians have read this in different ways.
b: This is the chapter's last word: the covenant survives judgment. Jewish readers have leaned on it through every dispersion; the rabbis said it means God would raise up leaders in every age, such as Daniel and Mordecai (Talmud, Megillah 11a). Paul asks, "did God push his people away? By no means!" (Romans 11:1) and says "God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:29). Christians who held that the church replaced Israel (supersessionism) read the promise as fulfilled in a spiritual Israel; many churches since the Holocaust affirm that God's covenant with the Jewish people still stands; the Catholic Catechism, building on Nostra Aetate (1965), says the Old Covenant "has never been revoked" (§121).

a: the laws that the LORD set between himself and the Israelites
p: The Holiness Code ends here. Torah means teaching or instruction, not only law.
b: This verse closes chapters 17–26, and many think it once closed the book (see 27:34). It names three kinds of instruction: chuqqim (rules), mishpatim (rulings) and torot (laws, plural of torah, literally "instructions"). The rabbis took the plural as two Torahs, the written and the oral, both given at Sinai (Sifra). "Between himself and the people" shows that law is relationship: the covenant has two sides.

a: an extraordinary vow
p: Yafli neder: to make a vow that stands out, a wonder-vow.
b: Yafli comes from the root of pele', "wonder." It marks a vow beyond the ordinary, especially vowing a person to God. Since people could not be sacrificed, the vow was paid in silver at a fixed value. Hannah vowed her son Samuel and gave him to serve at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:11, 28); Absalom made a vow at Hebron (2 Samuel 15:7–8). The Nazirite law uses the same verb (Numbers 6:2). The chapter is an appendix: 26:46 already closed the laws, and chapter 27 adds rules for gifts to the sanctuary.

a: fifty shekels of silver
t: What were the values based on?
p: The values match a person's work, not their worth. Readers have asked what they say about women.
b: The scale runs: men 20–60, fifty shekels; women, thirty; youths, twenty and ten; children, five and three; the old, fifteen and ten. Most scholars see the rates as labor value in a farm economy, roughly what slaves cost, not a judgment on human worth (Wenham). Fifty shekels was also the payment by a man who seized and lay with an unbetrothed virgin (Deuteronomy 22:28–29), and thirty the price of a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), the sum later paid to Judas (Matthew 26:15; Zechariah 11:12–13). An average worker earned perhaps a shekel a month, so a man's vow was a large sum. Feminist readers note the women's lower rate; others note that an old woman's value drops less than an old man's.

a: by what the one who vowed can afford
t: A sliding scale for the poor
p: The poor are not shut out of vowing. The priest sets a price they can pay.
b: As with the sacrifices, where the poor could bring birds or flour (5:7, 11; 12:8), the law adjusts to means. The rabbis said the priest leaves the poor man enough to live on, his bed, tools and food (Mishnah Arakhin 6:3). Mary and Joseph brought the poor family's offering at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:24).

a: both it and the animal put in its place will be holy
p: Once an animal is vowed, a trade makes both animals holy. The rule closes a loophole.
b: A worshiper who regretted vowing his best animal might try to substitute a lesser one. The law blocks this: both become God's. The Mishnah tractate Temurah, "Exchange," works out the rule in detail. Malachi condemns a man who "has a male in his flock and has made a vow, yet he sacrifices a spoiled animal to the Lord" (Malachi 1:14). The tithe has the same rule (27:33).

a: a homer of barley seed at fifty shekels of silver
p: Land was valued by how much seed it took to sow, over a full fifty-year cycle.
b: A homer, "a donkey load," was perhaps 50 gallons or more. The field's value is fifty shekels for the area a homer of barley could sow, over the full Jubilee period; most read this as one shekel per year. Since land returned at the Jubilee, a dedicated field was priced by the years left (27:18). Mesopotamian documents also measure fields by seed.

a: like a field under the ban
p: Cherem means something given wholly and finally to God. In war it meant destruction.
b: Cherem is the strongest form of dedication: what is devoted cannot be bought back (27:28). In peacetime it means property given permanently to the sanctuary or priests (Numbers 18:14; Ezekiel 44:29). In war it meant the "ban": everything in a conquered city given to God by destruction, as at Jericho (Joshua 6:17–21) and in Saul's war with Amalek (1 Samuel 15:3). The Moabite king Mesha's inscription (about 840 BC) boasts that he "devoted" an Israelite town to his god Ashtar-Kemosh (line 17), using the same word. Modern readers find the war ban among the Bible's hardest teachings.

a: No human being who has been put under the ban may be ransomed. He must be put to death.
p: Does this verse allow vowing a human life? Readers have answered no, and tied it to war or the courts.
b: The verse follows rules for gifts, so it can sound as if a person could vow another to death. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, reject that reading. Many tie it to the war ban, where those under cherem could not be spared (1 Samuel 15:3, 9), or to a person condemned by a court, whose life no vow can redeem. Jephthah vowed "whatever comes out" of his house and offered his daughter (Judges 11:30–39); a midrash says he could have redeemed her by the values of this chapter, but he and the high priest Phinehas were too proud to go to each other (Genesis Rabbah 60:3). The Bible elsewhere condemns child sacrifice outright (18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31).

a: All the tithe of the land
p: Leviticus gives the tithe to the LORD; Numbers to the Levites; Deuteronomy to a feast and the poor.
b: Numbers 18:21–24 gives the tithe to the Levites. Deuteronomy 14:22–29 tells farmers to eat their tithe at the sanctuary with family and Levites, and every third year to store it for the poor. The rabbis concluded there were several tithes: the first tithe for the Levites, the second eaten in Jerusalem, and the poor tithe in years three and six (Tobit 1:6–8 and Josephus, Antiquities 4.240, already know more than one). Critical scholars see different laws from different times. Jesus criticized careful tithing of herbs alongside neglect of "justice, mercy and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23). Christians still debate whether the tithe binds the church.
r: Genesis 14:20; Genesis 28:22; Numbers 18:21–28; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Malachi 3:8–10; Matthew 23:23; Hebrews 7:4–9

a: every tenth one of all that pass under the rod
p: The shepherd counted animals as they filed past his staff, and marked every tenth.
b: Shepherds counted the flock by having the animals pass one by one under the rod (Jeremiah 33:13). The Mishnah describes the tenth animal being marked with red paint (Bekhorot 9:7). Ezekiel uses the image for God judging and gathering Israel: "I will make you pass beneath the rod, and I will bring you into the covenant's bond" (Ezekiel 20:37). Choosing by count, not by eye, prevents keeping the best for oneself (27:33).

a: These are the commands that the LORD gave Moses
p: The book ends with vows and tithes. Why end there?
b: After the high drama of blessing and curse, Leviticus closes with a technical chapter on gifts to God. Many critical scholars think chapter 27 was added after 26:46 had closed the book. Others see a fitting close: the covenant ends with people freely giving themselves, their houses, fields and harvests to God, and the book's last word, Sinai, points back to the mountain where it all began. When a book of the Torah is finished in synagogue, the congregation calls out, "Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened" (chazak chazak venitchazek).
